recommendations.question: Q1
recommendations.decision: Make Python Stream A engine-agnostic. The suite owns the canonical IR and a reference evaluator: exact ML and REML for Gaussian LMMs with weights and offsets, and Laplace plus scalar AGQ for GLMMs. Engines only supply estimates, through thin adapters that must pass an objective-match test before any diagnostic runs. Version 1 ships three things. (1) A supported statsmodels MixedLM adapter, mainly to diagnose fits users already have, within what MixedLM can represent: one grouping factor with correlated slopes, nested variance components, and crossed intercepts or zero-correlation terms for modest n. (2) Experimental optional adapters for glmm and mixedlm: pip extras with pinned version ranges, run weekly in CI against their latest releases. These are the only Python engines found that cover the lme4 scope: crossed correlated slopes, weights, offsets, and Laplace and AGQ GLMMs. (3) A documented bring-your-own-estimates protocol (a dict or JSON in the contract schema) for any other engine. No dependency on pymer4, juliacall or gpboost. A direct rpy2-to-lme4 bridge is used only in monorepo CI for live cross-language parity tests.
recommendations.rationale:
The benchmark covered 27 models: the nine requested designs, with ML, REML and zero-correlation variants, a 12,000-row crossed design, a Bernoulli crossed GLMM and a J <= q design. All were evaluated under one engine-independent objective, which reproduces lme4 and glmmTMB criteria to within 4e-10.
- glmm 0.8.0 and mixedlm 1.3.0 reached the best objective on 27/27 models (gaps <= 5.5e-9). Fixed effects were within 5.3e-3 SE units of lme4, and LMM SEs within 6e-5 relative.
- glmm was about 14x faster than lme4 on warm refits and about 3x faster on first calls and on the 12,000-row model. mixedlm was 2.5x slower (median).
- statsmodels could fit 19/27 models. It cannot represent crossed correlated slopes, weights, offsets or likelihood-based GLMMs. It reached the optimum on all 13 interior LMMs but stopped 0.013 to 1.16 deviance units short on all 4 near-singular designs, twice reporting converged.
- statsmodels needed 16 to 43 s and 155 s for crossed variance-component models that lme4 fits in 0.12 s and 0.87 s.
- Its Bayesian GLMMs are not likelihood fits. Variational-Bayes posterior SDs were 52% below lme4 SEs, and the MAP fit collapsed the herd SD to zero, 14 units off the optimum.
- Both Rust engines are under 11 months old, each has a single maintainer, and both changed behaviour or APIs between minor releases. mixedlm 1.3.0 changed its default optimiser and its GLMM estimation; glmm 0.7.0 and 0.8.0 removed public names, with roughly weekly releases. Neither can safely be a hard dependency.
- An engine-agnostic design confines churn to roughly 100-line adapters and lets the suite catch engine failures. The objective-match test exposed gpboost's approximate default likelihood, glmmTMB's different weight semantics, lme4 1.1-35's missing AGQ constants, and a vech-unpacking bug in my own glmm adapter.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: 8/27 benchmark models are unrepresentable (crossed correlated slopes, weights, offsets, GLMM MLE). It stopped short on 4/4 near-singular designs (2 flagged converged), was 130 to 313x slower than lme4 on crossed designs, and 0.15.0 brought only bug fixes to MixedLM since 2023.

Its docs say 'Do NOT use pip' and the wheel declares no dependencies. Import failed here because the R package broom.mixed was missing (it also needs emmeans, tidyverse, arrow, report and parameters). rpy2 is tightly coupled to the R version: 3.6.7+ requires R >= 4.5, and older rpy2 cannot work with R >= 4.6. No release since May 2025 and 2 commits in 12 months.

ML only and independent random slopes only. Its default iterative likelihood is approximate (0.13 to 0.67 deviance units from exact), and it stops short of the optimum: gap up to 0.12 by default and 3.4e-3 even in Cholesky mode.
A strong engine, but every user would need a Julia runtime and precompilation, it has no denominator df, it could not be tested here, and it adds a third language for one maintainer.

alternatives_rejected.option: glmm or mixedlm as a hard dependency or the default engine
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Single maintainers, less than a year old, and breaking or behaviour-changing releases.

alternatives_rejected.option: Use the shared glmm/fastglmm engine as the parity mechanism
alternatives_rejected.why_not: fastglmm is on R-universe, not CRAN, so the CRAN package cannot rely on it. The reference objective defines parity for any pair of engines instead.

recommendations.revisit_if: A Rust engine meets the promotion rule (Q1.later); statsmodels gains weights, offsets or crossed covariance blocks; fastglmm reaches CRAN; or HPC conformance runs show glmm or mixedlm converging to non-optimal points at a materially higher rate than lme4.

recommendations.question: Q1.later
recommendations.decision: In v1.x, add Python GLMM diagnostics through the experimental adapters, with GLMM SEs recomputed by the suite under one declared convention. In v2, promote at most one Rust engine to 'supported', and make it the documented default for new Python fits, only when three conditions hold: the conformance corpus passes at tolerance tier on 3 consecutive upstream releases; the fields the adapter reads have not broken for 12 months; and the upstream has a second active maintainer or an institutional home. Add a juliacall adapter only on user demand. Keep a small suite-side verification optimiser (profiled REML or ML over theta with boundary restarts, small q) for boundary probes and for diagnosing objective-match failures, not as a production engine.
recommendations.rationale: The proposal stages GLMMs after Gaussian LMMs, and statsmodels has no frequentist GLMM. Both Rust engines matched lme4 and glmmTMB on all 5 GLMMs, including a Bernoulli crossed model with a correlated by-subject slope. GLMM SE conventions differ by up to 2.2% between engines, so the suite should own vcov. The statsmodels boundary failures show that a suite-side probe is needed. Neither Rust engine meets the promotion criteria today.

alternatives_rejected.option: Build a full in-house fitting engine
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Too large for one maintainer and duplicates lme4-grade numerics. An evaluator plus a small verification optimiser is enough for parity and diagnostics.

alternatives_rejected.option: Wait for statsmodels to grow the needed features
alternatives_rejected.why_not: The 0.15.0 release notes (2023-05 to 2026-08) list only MixedLM bug fixes.

recommendations.revisit_if: Maintainer capacity grows (co-maintainers), or user demand concentrates on one engine.

recommendations.question: Q1.contract
recommendations.rationale:
Each field answers an observed discrepancy:
- glmmTMB 1.1.8 treats Gaussian weights as log-likelihood multipliers (sigma 0.85 against 2.06 in lme4): a different model, not a different optimum.
- gpboost's default likelihood is approximate.
- lme4 1.1-35's AGQ log-likelihood lacks constants (84 and 1,681 units off).
- SE conventions split: statsmodels and glmmTMB use the joint Hessian, 2.4% off on a school-level predictor; GLMM SEs differ by up to 2.2% between engines.
- mixedlm names coefficients f.1/f.2 (level labels lost), returns BLUPs without level labels, and drops a different aliased column from lme4; statsmodels drops none.
- glmm packs covariances column-major, and a row-major reading went unnoticed until a 3x3 block failed the objective-match test.
- glmm and gpboost expose no Z, so the suite must rebuild designs from its own IR.
- All engines agree on the beta-fixed conditional variance (within 3e-6 to 5e-5 of exact), whereas the PEV with beta uncertainty differs by up to 1.7%, so the two must be labelled.

alternatives_rejected.option: A contract of point estimates only
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It cannot detect non-optimal stopping, packing errors or a different likelihood (catalogue L4-02 makes the same point).
Contradicted four times in this benchmark: lme4 AGQ constants, gpboost's approximate likelihood, glmmTMB weights, and statsmodels reporting converged at worse optima.

alternatives_rejected.option: Requiring Z and an objective callable from every engine
alternatives_rejected.why_not: glmm and gpboost expose neither; the suite rebuilds Z from the IR and evaluates its own objective.

recommendations.revisit_if: Multi-component engines (glmmTMB zero-inflation or dispersion models) or residual correlation structures enter scope. The contract then needs the per-component dimension of catalogue L6-06.

recommendations.question: Q1.tiers
recommendations.decision:
Assign parity tiers per (engine, version range, output class) from the conformance corpus, never a priori, and record them in the expected-disagreement registry (catalogue L4-20). Tolerance tier: common objective within max(1e-4, 1e-9*|dev|) of the best, and beta within 1e-2 SE units. SEs reach tolerance tier only between engines with the same vcov convention, or after the suite recomputes vcov. Initial assignment:
- glmm 0.8.0 and mixedlm 1.3.0: tolerance for LMM and GLMM (Laplace and AGQ) estimates and objective, and for LMM SEs. mixedlm GLMM SEs are engine-specific; glmm GLMM SEs equal glmmTMB's.
- statsmodels 0.15.0: tolerance for interior Gaussian LMMs. Engine-specific near the boundary (to be flagged by the suite's probe) and for SEs (joint Hessian). Unavailable for crossed correlated slopes, weights, offsets and GLMM MLE; its Bayesian GLMMs are engine-specific.
- gpboost: engine-specific, Cholesky mode 'near'.
- glmmTMB 1.1.8 (R): tolerance except weights (a different model) and false convergence on crossed_ML, which the suite flags.
- lme4 before 2.1-0: AGQ log-likelihood is engine-specific.
Full table: contract_and_tiers.md.
recommendations.rationale: One tier per engine would be wrong: statsmodels is at the optimum on all 13 interior LMMs but 0.013 to 1.16 units off on 4/4 near-singular designs. Coordinate-wise tolerances would fail healthy fits because of SE conventions (2.4% and 2.2%) and boundary SDs. Objective-first comparison separated every case cleanly.

alternatives_rejected.option: Exact or coefficient-wise parity across languages
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Fails on SE conventions and boundary fits, and depends on the version (lme4 1.1-35 against 2.1-0).

recommendations.revisit_if: The HPC conformance runs with current CRAN versions (lme4 2.1-0, glmmTMB 1.1.15.2) change any assignment.

recommendations.question: Q1.validation-paper
recommendations.decision: Commit this benchmark as the seed conformance corpus: CSV fixtures, R reference JSON, the Python reference objective, and the expected-disagreement registry entries found here. Extend it on ARC htc into a simulation study: each design replicated hundreds of times, current engine versions, and large-n timing and memory runs, with results in /data/educ-intract/educ1242/. Report per-engine rates of non-optimal convergence with Monte Carlo SEs and preregistered tolerance thresholds, and make objective-first cross-engine conformance a section of the software paper.
recommendations.rationale: One replicate per design already exposed four classes of disagreement and one adapter bug. Estimating failure rates, such as statsmodels stopping short near the boundary or glmmTMB false convergence, needs replicates and is heavy enough for HPC. The corpus doubles as the CI conformance suite that gates adapter promotion.

alternatives_rejected.option: Rely on the engines' own validation claims
alternatives_rejected.why_not: glmm's 947-model grid is run by hand, not in CI, against older oracles (lme4 2.0-6, glmmTMB 1.1.14). mixedlm's claims are untested here beyond these 27 models.

recommendations.revisit_if: Never: the corpus should run before each release of the suite.

evidence.claim: The engine-independent reference objective (ML and REML with weights, Laplace and AGQ) reproduces lme4 1.1-35.1 and glmmTMB 1.1.8 criteria at their own estimates.
evidence.result: All LMMs agree within 4e-10 (including weighted lmer); Laplace agrees with glmmTMB to 1.5e-12. lme4's reported glmer logLik is 5.6e-4 (cbpp) and 2.9e-6 (owls) above the Laplace value at its own estimates.

evidence.claim: lme4 1.1-35.1 nAGQ = 25 log-likelihoods lack normalising constants (consistent with the lme4 2.1-0 NEWS entry cited in the proposal).
evidence.result: Reported -2logLik is 100.01 against a common AGQ objective of 183.97 (cbpp, 84 units), and 3521.9 against 5202.7 (owls, 1,681 units).

evidence.claim: glmm 0.8.0 and mixedlm 1.3.0 reach the best common objective on all 27 models.
evidence.result: 27/27 at the optimum for each. LMM gaps <= 5.5e-9 (glmm) and 1.5e-12 (mixedlm); GLMM gaps <= 6e-11. Fixed effects within 5.3e-3 SE units of lme4; LMM SEs within 6e-5 relative.

evidence.claim: statsmodels 0.15.0 MixedLM coverage and accuracy.
evidence.result: 19/27 fitted; 8 unsupported (crossed correlated slopes x4, weights x2, offsets x2). 13/13 interior LMMs at the optimum. All 4 near-singular designs stopped short (gaps 0.013, 0.14, 0.53, 1.16), two of them with converged = True.

evidence.claim: statsmodels is very slow on crossed designs, which it can fit only as variance components inside one all-data group.
evidence.result: 2,400 rows: 16 to 43 s per fit, against 0.12 s for lme4. 12,000 rows (460 random effects): 155 s against 0.87 s, peak RSS 583 MB.

evidence.claim: The statsmodels Bayesian mixed GLMs are not substitutes for likelihood GLMMs.
evidence.result: VB: intercept posterior SD 0.112 against lme4 SE 0.231 (-52%), objective gap 0.068. MAP: herd SD 0.000, gap 14.1. No offset argument; binary responses only; independent random effects only.

evidence.claim: Fixed-effect SE conventions differ between engines.
evidence.result: LMM: statsmodels and glmmTMB (joint observed Hessian) are 2.4% above lme4, glmm and mixedlm for the school-level predictor (0.3042 vs 0.2971). GLMM: glmm equals glmmTMB; lme4 1.1-35 differs by up to 1.3%; mixedlm by up to 2.2%.

evidence.claim: gpboost 1.8.0's default likelihood for grouped random effects is approximate, and its optimiser stops short.
evidence.result: With the default matrix_inversion_method, the likelihood differs from exact by 0.13 to 0.67 deviance units; with 'cholesky' the difference is <= 1.4e-12. Gap to the optimum up to 0.12 by default and up to 3.4e-3 with Cholesky. ML only; independent slopes only (D).

evidence.claim: glmmTMB 1.1.8 failures relevant to the R-side registry.
evidence.result: crossed_ML: gap 7.09, NA logLik, non-positive-definite Hessian, item slope variance 0.34 against 121.8. Gaussian weights act as log-likelihood multipliers (sigma 0.85 against 2.06), a different model. jq_REML: gap 0.014 with pdHess FALSE. Current CRAN 1.1.15.2 not tested.

evidence.claim: pymer4 0.9.2 cannot be installed by pip into a working state.
evidence.result: The wheel declares no dependencies and the docs say 'Do NOT use pip'. Import raises PackageNotInstalledError for broom.mixed; it also requires lmerTest, emmeans, tidyverse, broom, arrow and report. CRAN is unreachable here.

evidence.claim: rpy2 is tightly coupled to the R version.
evidence.result: rpy2 3.6.9 and 3.6.6 in ABI mode fail on R 4.3.3 (undefined symbol R_getVar). The 3.6.7 NEWS says R >= 4.5 is required and that R 4.6 hides C entry points. API mode failed at link (-ltirpc) even after apt-get install r-base-dev, which I ran. rpy2 3.5.17 ABI works; rpy2-to-lme4 gives identical estimates at a median 1.33x lme4 fit time.

evidence.claim: Handling of a rank-deficient X differs between engines.
evidence.result: With x3 = x1 + x2: glmm drops x3 and flags it, as lme4 does; mixedlm drops x2 and keeps x3; statsmodels drops nothing and returns unidentified estimates with converged = False.

evidence.claim: The default reference level and coefficient names differ between engines and R locales.
evidence.result: Labels b, a, C. glmm, mixedlm and statsmodels use C as reference. R uses C in the C locale but a in C.UTF-8. mixedlm names the coefficients f.1 and f.2, losing the level labels.

evidence.claim: Conditional variances of random effects agree across engines under the beta-fixed definition.
evidence.result: lme4 equals the exact beta-fixed conditional variance to 5e-15. glmm, mixedlm and statsmodels match lme4 within 3.3e-6 (sleepstudy) and 4.5e-5 (school). The PEV including beta uncertainty differs by up to 1.7%. mixedlm returns only per-term variances, without level labels.

evidence.claim: The objective-match test catches adapter packing errors that 2x2 fixtures cannot.
evidence.source: bench/engines.py (fit_glmm, column-major fix); glmm/__init__.py lines 643 and 933 (column-major vech)
evidence.result: A row-major reading of glmm's 3x3 varcorr gave a reference REML criterion 2.32 units above glmm's reported criterion. After the column-major fix the gap is 8.5e-14.

evidence.claim: Speed relative to lme4, timed in-process for the fit only on a 4-core container.
evidence.result: Median ratio to lme4 (warm fits): glmm 0.07 (range 0.02 to 0.3; first calls 0.33), mixedlm 2.5 (0.37 to 27), statsmodels 5.4 (1.3 to 313), glmmTMB 13, gpboost 16 to 23 (4 threads), rpy2-to-lme4 1.33.

evidence.claim: Capabilities verified by direct calls.
evidence.result: mixedlm: getME X/Z/theta, as_function(theta) equals REMLcrit, simulate, bootMer, Satterthwaite and KR df. glmm: Satterthwaite df, postvar, simulate, profile CIs; no Z, no objective callable, no KR. statsmodels: no simulate, no df, rejects weights. gpboost: neg_log_likelihood callable; no REML.

evidence.claim: Release history, licences and maintainers.
evidence.source: pypi/*.json via pypi_summary.py; git/glmm.git, git/mixedlm.git, git/GPBoost.git, git/pymer4.git (treeless clones)
evidence.result: mixedlm: 6 releases since 2026-01-13, MIT, one human author (1,106 commits). glmm: 14 releases since 2026-07-16, LGPL-3.0-or-later, one author (69/70 commits). gpboost: 94 releases since 2020, Apache-2.0, mainly one maintainer. pymer4: last release 2025-05-28, 2 commits in 12 months. statsmodels: BSD-3, 0.15.0 on 2026-08-27.

evidence.claim: Upstream behaviour changes and validation practice.
evidence.result: mixedlm 1.3.0 changed the default LMM optimiser and GLMM estimation ('estimates can change'). glmm 0.7.0 and 0.8.0 removed public names. glmm's lme4 comparison is run by hand, not in CI. statsmodels 0.15.0 brought only MixedLM bug fixes.

evidence.claim: MixedModels.jl capabilities, from documentation only (not run).
evidence.source: gh/mmjl_README.md, gh/mmjl_NEWS.md, gh/mmjl_docs_src_constructors.md, gh/mmjl_docs_src_bootstrap.md, gh/mmjl_docs_src_api.md, gh/mmjl_Project.toml
evidence.result: Version 5.9.1 on main. ML is the default and REML optional. Provides zerocorr, AGQ for a single scalar term only, fast, weights, a GLMM offset, condVar, parametricbootstrap and issingular. No Satterthwaite or KR anywhere in the fetched docs.

recommendations.question: Q3.1 Single recommended formula, or ceiling + identifiability verdict + pre-specified ladder?
recommendations.decision: Do not return a single recommended formula. Stream B returns a plan object with five parts: (a) the design-implied ceiling per grouping factor, with informative-group counts and the level-specific df budget; (b) an identifiability verdict for the ceiling and for every rung (exact for Gaussian LMMs with unstructured, diagonal or cs covariances; a necessary condition only for GLMMs); (c) a deterministic, outcome-free ladder of nested rungs with an explicit protected set; (d) a stopping rule chosen from a registry menu, with a package default (Q3.3) and a declared terminal alternative; (e) a hash of all of this. The confirmatory model is defined as 'the output of rule R applied to ladder L', and the user, not the package, declares it primary. A single formula is emitted only when the ladder has one rung or the user chooses the rule 'no reduction'. Worked example: tables/streamB_q3_contract_example.json.
recommendations.rationale: (1) There is no consensus. The lme4 documentation states 'There is not yet consensus about how to deal with singularity, or more generally to choose which random-effects specification ... to use' and lists five strategies. Barr et al. (2013), Bates et al. (2015), Matuschek et al. (2017), Scandola and Tidoni (2024) and the Bayesian literature (Oberauer, 2022; van Doorn et al., 2023, where invited experts disagreed strongly) recommend different procedures. (2) No formula dominates, because the best structure depends on slope variances that only the outcome reveals. In Sim 1 (24 subjects x 16 items), the maximal model kept Type I error at .016-.037 but had 5-8 fewer power points than selection rules when slopes varied little. Intercepts-only had the most power but a Type I error of .200 (.348 in the 48 x 32 design). (3) Practice varies widely (Meteyard & Davies, 2020: a survey of 163 researchers and a review of 400 papers), and analytic flexibility changes conclusions (Coretta et al., 2023: 46 teams; Roettger, 2019). A pre-specified procedure removes the degrees of freedom that a suggested formula would leave. (4) A formula labelled as recommended by the package would be cited as an endorsement, whereas a recorded rule can be audited.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: The maximal fit was singular in 27-83% of Sim 1 data sets and the formula gives no rule for failures, so users then reduce ad hoc.

alternatives_rejected.option: Return one data-driven formula (rePCA- or LRT-based, as in Bates et al. 2015, buildmer or lmerTest::step)
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It needs the outcome, so it cannot be produced outcome-blind, and the reduction order itself depends on the outcome. lmerTest::step also eliminates fixed effects by default (alpha.fixed = 0.05).

alternatives_rejected.option: Ceiling and verdict without a ladder
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It leaves reduction to judgement after the data are seen, which is where flexibility enters.

recommendations.revisit_if: HPC study H1 shows a single rule with Type I error at or below .06 and the highest power across all core designs. Current evidence makes this unlikely.

recommendations.question: Q3.2 Ladder ordering
recommendations.decision: Build the ladder from T0 information only (roles, design, coding), in this order. Step 0, preconditions: freeze coding (deviation or sum codes as numeric contrast columns) and centring constants, and record which sample they came from. Rung 0 is the ceiling restricted to identifiable terms. Protected set (never removed by the ladder): random intercepts of replication and randomisation units; by-unit slopes of focal within-unit effects; for a focal interaction, the slope for the highest-order combination of within-unit factors it contains (Barr, 2013); the lower-level slope of any focal cross-level interaction. Ordering keys for the remaining terms: k1, simplify covariance before removing variances, starting with the grouping factor that has fewer informative groups. Factor slopes with 3 or more levels go from unstructured to compound symmetry (cs/homcs, or complex random intercepts), which is defined on cells and so does not depend on the coding; numeric columns go to diag. k2, nuisance slopes before anything protected, and higher-order terms before their marginal terms. k3, among nuisance slopes, drop first those uncorrelated with focal predictors within units and with homogeneous cluster composition (low predictor ICC), then those on grouping factors with fewer informative groups. k4, stop at the protected set; if that rung fails, apply the declared terminal alternative instead of removing protected terms. An 'unprotected tail' is available only by explicit opt-in and is flagged in the report.
recommendations.rationale: Nuisance before focal: in Sim 3, dropping the focal slope gave Type I error of .226 (r = 0) and .187 (r = .5), while dropping a nuisance slope gave .054 and .035. This agrees with Barr (2013), where intercepts-only gave .170-.267 for interactions against .063-.064 for the maximal model, and with Scandola and Tidoni (2024), who found that excluding a within-subject factor or interaction inflates Type I error. Protecting cross-level slopes: in Sim 2 with 15 clusters, LRT(.2) and AIC removed the lower-level slope often enough to reach .064-.073, while keeping it gave .042-.051. Heisig and Schaeffer (2019) report severe anticonservatism, and Luo and Li (2023) favour maximal or best-path searches for within-cluster and cross-level focal effects. Correlations first is standard practice (the Bates et al. procedure in the RePsychLing vignette; the afex vignette) and removes the least precisely estimated parameters. However, zero-correlation fits changed the REML criterion (1773.66 vs 1774.99), slope SE (.1031 vs .1007) and df (31.3 vs 29.0) between 0/1 and +-0.5 coding (Sim 4; also Frossard & Renaud, 2019), hence coding is frozen first and cs is used for multi-level factors. In lme4 1.1-35.1, '(1 + f || g)' with a factor kept 7 parameters, including correlations among indicators; lme4 2.0-1 added diag() and cs() and recommends diag() explicitly. Keeping correlated nuisance slopes longer: with r = .5, dropping the nuisance slope raised the mean SE from .0741 to .0795 and lowered power from .482 to .447 (Sim 3). Verissimo (2023) and Heisig et al. (2017) report inflated evidence or lost precision when such slopes are omitted. Fixed versus data-driven order made no measurable difference in Sim 1 (LRT(.2) Type I .045 vs .043, power .318 vs .320 at tau = .4), so outcome-free ordering costs little.

alternatives_rejected.option: Data-driven order, smallest estimated variance first (Bates et al. 2015; afex; buildmer)
alternatives_rejected.why_not: The order depends on the outcome and can remove focal slopes.

alternatives_rejected.option: Order by J_eff alone (earlier draft of the proposal)
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It can remove focal slopes before nuisance slopes (catalogue L1-17 correction).

alternatives_rejected.option: Use '||' on factors as the correlation step
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It is redundant or unidentified for factors in lme4's default expansion (Sim 4), and its meaning differs between engines.
It removes more information first, and there is no evidence of benefit.

recommendations.revisit_if: HPC study H2 shows that the order among nuisance terms, or cs versus diag rungs, changes focal Type I error or power by more than 2 Monte Carlo SEs. Also revisit if the Luo and Li (2023) versus Heisig et al. (2017) conflict resolves differently from key k3.

recommendations.question: Q3.3 Default stopping rule and how to preregister it
recommendations.decision: Default for confirmatory use: SR-P, 'protected fit-failure back-off'. Walk the ladder from rung 0. Accept an unprotected rung only if two registry-defined criteria hold: it converged (suite-computed scaled gradient and Hessian checks, with a second optimiser confirming the objective), and no random-effects covariance block is rank-deficient (scale-free tolerance); otherwise step down. Accept the protected rung even when singular, naming the zero-variance directions. If the protected rung fails convergence after the second-optimiser check, apply the declared terminal alternative, for example a penalised (MAP) covariance prior, or CR2 inference for nested designs, labelled as an alternative estimator. Engine warnings never decide a step on their own. Registered alternatives, each carrying its evidence in the registry: SR-U (unprotected back-off along the same ladder); SR-LRT(.2) along the same ladder, applied by default to unprotected terms only (REML, naive chi-square); SR-AIC; SR-none (keep the ceiling); SR-Bayes (declared priors, no ladder). Preregistration: Stream B writes the plan as canonical JSON plus generated text. The hash covers the design, coding and centring constants, ladder, protected set, rule ID and version, engine, version and optimiser settings, terminal alternative, deferred checks and reporting commitments. The user deposits the plan (for example on OSF). Stream A reports the selected model as primary, the protected or ceiling rung and the adjacent rung as pre-declared sensitivity analyses, and a deviation table in the format of Willroth and Atherton (2024) and Lakens (2024).
recommendations.rationale: Type I error across my conditions. Both back-off rules stayed between .018 and .059 in every cell: the protected rule gave .018-.040 (Sim 1, small design) and .044-.056 (large design); keeping the slope gave .032-.051 in Sim 2; unprotected back-off gave .031-.058. LRT(.2) and AIC were near nominal in the crossed design (.033-.060) but reached .064-.073 for a focal cross-level slope with 15 clusters. LRT(.05) reached .080 and intercepts-only .348. Why the default is protected: SR-U decides focal slopes from singular flags that depend on tolerance, units and engine (catalogue L4-04, L4-05). Its extra power (4-7 points in the 24 x 16 design at tau <= .2, for example .560 vs .517 at tau = 0; 1.4 points in the 48 x 32 design) does not come from removing zero-variance terms, which Sim 6 showed to be inference-neutral (SE ratio within 3e-6, df 22.2 vs 22.2, rejection .59 vs .59). It comes from the fixed ladder also removing small non-zero slopes when another term is singular, which is the same mechanism that made LRT(.2) and AIC anticonservative in Sim 2. In GLMMs, non-convergence also occurs with known non-zero variances (Eager & Roy, 2017: 82% for complex logistic models in lme4 at that time, against Bates et al.'s view that it usually signals excess complexity), so a back-off rule that can remove focal slopes is riskier there. Published support for selection rules is limited to LRT and AIC (Matuschek et al., 2017; Seedorff et al., 2019, a preprint), and marginal AIC is biased towards dropping random effects (Greven & Kneib, 2010). The cost of protection is bounded: at most 7 power points in the small design and about 1 point in the larger one.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: It was anticonservative for focal cross-level slopes with few clusters (.064-.070 in Sim 2) and needs an alpha. The value .2 is attributed to the paper only by a secondary source and is not confirmed from the full text.
It showed the same few-cluster inflation (.070-.073) and is biased towards smaller random structures (Greven & Kneib 2010).

alternatives_rejected.option: LRT(.05) (for example the reduction step in the Bates et al. vignette)
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It was anticonservative (.068-.080) in Sim 1 at tau >= .2.

alternatives_rejected.option: SR-U, unprotected singular-or-nonconvergent back-off, as default
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It was competitive in Sims 1-2, but its focal decisions depend on the engine and tolerance and it is untested in GLMMs. It is kept as a registered alternative pending HPC study H1/H4.

alternatives_rejected.option: Bayesian or regularised fit as default
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It needs prior choices and evidence of frequentist calibration (H10), which is too much scope for one maintainer in release 1.

recommendations.revisit_if: Switch the default if HPC studies H1, H4 or H5 show either of two things. First, SR-P above .06 in any core cell (2,000 replicates, MCSE about .005), for example through df behaviour at singular fits. Second, a rule that stays at or below .06 everywhere while giving at least 3 more power points on average across cells with tau > 0. Bradley's (1978) liberal band of .025-.075 is a coarse screen only.

recommendations.question: Q3.4 Should outcome-blind operation be the default, and how should T1 and T2 checks be unlocked and logged?
recommendations.decision: Yes, Stream B runs outcome-blind (T0) by default, because the ceiling, verdict, ladder and plan need no outcome. T1 checks (outcome read marginally or by cluster) unlock only through an explicit outcome_access = 'marginal' together with the hash of a frozen T0 plan. Without a plan, T1 runs in a mode labelled exploratory, and any plan created afterwards is stamped 'planned after outcome-marginal inspection'. T2 checks (outcome related to predictors or a fitted model) run only in Stream A or in an explicit exploratory mode. Every unlock is logged as an append-only, hash-chained record: timestamp, tier, check IDs, outcome-column hash, plan hash, package and registry versions, stated reason, and a prior-knowledge attestation (for secondary data). A plan revised after any unlock gets a new hash that points to its parent, with a diff, and the report header shows the highest tier accessed before the plan was frozen. T1 and T2 checks can be preregistered as deferred checks with decision rules based on effect sizes, not p-values. A change made outside those rules is reported as a deviation, with the preregistered model shown next to the adapted one. Masked execution: for Gaussian LMMs, Stream A can run the stopping rule on y + X_focal b, with b secret, or on y residualised on the focal columns. It fixes the rung, logs it, and only then unmasks. GLMMs are excluded until validated.
recommendations.rationale: Blind analysis fixes decisions before results are seen and labels later analyses as post-blind (MacCoun & Perlmutter, 2015; Dutilh et al., 2021). In a comparison of 120 teams, blinding took about as long as preregistration, and blinded teams could plan analyses they deviated from less (Sarafoglou et al., 2023). Every stopping rule reads y through the fitted models, so it can be made pre-specified and logged, but not free of the outcome. Masking makes it blind to the focal effect. Gaussian LMM likelihoods, REML and profiled ML alike, depend on y only through residuals orthogonal to X. In Sim 5, refitting with y + 3.7A changed theta by at most .001 and the REML criterion by at most 1.7e-4, with identical singular and warning flags in 799 of 800 fits; the rare flips sat at a numerical threshold, which the registry's 'near threshold' status covers. Limits recorded in the catalogue (L1-16, L3-21, L6-22): T0 cannot certify separation, outcome-type adequacy or missingness in the outcome; the declared family is itself an assumption; outcome-blindness is an attestation, not an enforced guarantee. Secondary data may already be known to the analyst (van den Akker et al., 2021).

alternatives_rejected.why_not: It invites forking paths before the plan is fixed.

alternatives_rejected.option: Enforcing blindness by detecting and refusing outcome columns
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Detection is unreliable, since columns can be renamed. Use an attestation plus hashes instead.

alternatives_rejected.option: Masked execution for GLMMs in release 1
alternatives_rejected.why_not: The invariance is not exact under a non-identity link. This is HPC study H9.

recommendations.revisit_if: If most users analyse secondary data, make the prior-knowledge attestation mandatory but keep T0 as the default. If H9 shows approximately invariant masking for GLMMs, extend masked execution to them.

recommendations.question: Q3.5 What does the literature leave unsettled that needs HPC simulation, and which conditions should vary?
recommendations.decision: Run a preregistered simulation study on ARC htc using SLURM job arrays, with outputs in /data/educ-intract/educ1242/. Follow the ADEMP structure (Morris et al., 2019) and the ADEMP-PreReg template (Siepe et al., 2024). Priority: H1, all rules applied to the same fixed ladder in crossed designs; H5, education designs with few clusters (cross-level and level-2 effects; protected ladder vs RI + CR2 vs fixed grouping vs REML with t df); H4, GLMMs (Bernoulli and Poisson; is non-convergence evidence of over-parameterisation with current lme4 2.x and glmmTMB?); H2, ordering among nuisance terms (within-unit correlation with the focal predictor, compositional heterogeneity, level of the focal effect); H3, registry singular and convergence criteria (scaling, tolerance, cross-engine agreement). Then H6 (calibration of outcome-blind design analysis), H7 (post-selection reporting), H8 (engine parity of the rung reached), H9 (masking for GLMMs) and H10 (calibration of Bayesian and penalised terminal alternatives). Factors and levels are in tables/hpc_simulation_plan.tsv: subjects 12-96, items 8-64, clusters 6-80, slope-to-residual SD 0-.8, correlations 0-.9, MCAR missingness 0-.3, cluster-size CV 0-1, deviation vs treatment coding, three engines, and Satterthwaite, KR, LRT or parametric-bootstrap inference. Use 2,000 replicates per H0 cell (MCSE about .005) and 1,000 per H1 cell, with a fractional factorial design plus a metamodel.
recommendations.rationale: No published simulation tests back-off on singular or non-convergent fits as a rule (my searches found none, and the lme4 documentation lists it without evidence). Matuschek et al. (2017) cover a narrow crossed design. The Bates et al. (2015) and Eager and Roy (2017) conflict about non-convergence predates the current engines. Luo and Li (2023) and Heisig et al. (2017) conflict on level-1 slopes for level-2 effects. Few-cluster calibration differs between methods (Huang & Zhang, 2025; Zhang & Lai, 2024; Elff et al., 2021). Engine-independent criteria and masking are new. My small simulations, run with lme4 1.1-35.1 at about 0.07 s per lmer fit on 384 rows, support rough costs of about 200 CPU-hours for the Gaussian core grid, about 400 for GLMMs, about 100 for ordering and about 200 for MCMC, roughly 800-1,300 CPU-hours in total.

alternatives_rejected.option: A full factorial over all factors
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It is computationally excessive and not manageable for one maintainer.

alternatives_rejected.option: Fewer than 1,000 replicates per H0 cell
alternatives_rejected.why_not: An MCSE of about .007 cannot resolve the .05 vs .06 differences that decide the default.

recommendations.revisit_if: Re-plan if early H1 cells show all rules within the tolerance and with similar power; then shrink H2 and H3 and move effort to GLMMs (H4).

recommendations.question: Q3.6 Scope for one maintainer and the paper
recommendations.decision: Release 1 of Q3 should include: the ladder generator from the canonical IR and declared roles; the per-rung identifiability verdict (reusing catalogue L1-06); three rules (SR-P as default, SR-LRT(.2) on unprotected terms, SR-none); the plan hash and generated preregistration text; the outcome-access log; and masked execution for Gaussian LMMs in R (lme4). In Python, cover the rungs that statsmodels can express; complex random intercepts should map to variance components, which is untested. Defer to release 2 or later: Bayesian and MAP terminal alternatives (documented only), model averaging (Heck & Bockting; Martinez-Huertas & Olmos, 2022), masking for GLMMs, and cs rungs for engines that lack them. Paper: a methods and software article built on H1, H2, H4 and H5, with the simulation protocol preregistered before the runs.
recommendations.rationale: The default rule and its validation are the novel, citable parts. Everything else either already exists in other packages (buildmer, lmerTest::step, afex) or needs prior-elicitation machinery that one maintainer cannot support well.

alternatives_rejected.option: Ship all registered rules and Bayesian alternatives in release 1
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Too large a validation and support burden without co-maintainers.

recommendations.revisit_if: A co-maintainer joins, or HPC results make SR-U or LRT(.2) the better default.

evidence.claim: In a small crossed design, the choice of stopping rule moves Type I error from conservative to anticonservative
evidence.result: 24 subjects x 16 items, 1,000 replicates per cell, Satterthwaite tests (lme4 1.1-35.1, lmerTest 3.1-3). Type I error for tau = 0/.1/.2/.4: maximal .025/.016/.037/.037; protected .032/.018/.040/.037; back-off on singular or non-convergent .043/.031/.055/.050; LRT(.2) .044/.033/.057/.043; AIC .047/.036/.059/.055; LRT(.05) .055/.042/.068/.080; intercepts only .059/.043/.084/.200.

evidence.claim: The maximal and protected rules cost power in small designs when slope variance is small
With more subjects and items, the differences between valid rules shrink
evidence.result: 48 x 32, 500 replicates. Type I error at tau = .2/.4: maximal and protected .044/.056; back-off .052/.058; LRT(.2) .052/.056; AIC .060/.056; LRT(.05) .080/.056; intercepts only .146/.348. Power at tau = .2: maximal .712, protected .710, back-off .724, LRT(.2) .724-.728, AIC .738.

evidence.claim: A fixed, outcome-free order loses nothing against a data-driven order (smallest variance first) in this design
evidence.result: LRT(.2) with design order vs data-driven order: Type I .045 vs .043 at tau = .4 and .055 vs .057 at tau = .2; power .318 vs .320 at tau = .4.

evidence.claim: Singular maximal fits are common when slope variance is small; convergence warnings are rare in Gaussian LMMs
evidence.result: Maximal fit singular (isSingular, tolerance 1e-4) in 83/79/67/27% of data sets at tau = 0/.1/.2/.4 (24 x 16), and in 29% and 0.4% at tau = .2/.4 (48 x 32). Convergence warnings 1.0-4.0%.

evidence.claim: Data-driven removal of the lower-level slope inflates Type I error for a cross-level interaction when clusters are few; protection prevents it
Dropping a nuisance slope before the focal slope keeps the focal test valid; correlated nuisance slopes carry information
evidence.result: Under H0, r = 0: full .059, drop nuisance .054, drop focal .226. Under H0, r = .5: .039/.035/.187. With r = .5, power for full vs drop-nuisance was .482 vs .447, and mean SE .0741 vs .0795.

evidence.claim: Zero-correlation models depend on coding, and '||' with a factor is redundant in lme4 1.1-35.1
evidence.result: Unstructured model: identical REML criterion (1773.273) and slope SE (.10072) under 0/1 and +-0.5 coding. Zero-correlation model: REML criterion 1773.664 vs 1774.988, SE .10306 vs .10072, df 31.3 vs 29.0. '(1 + f3 || s)' kept 7 covariance parameters; numeric sum-contrast columns kept 3.

evidence.claim: Likelihood-based random-effects selection in Gaussian LMMs is invariant to the focal fixed effect, which enables masked ladder execution
evidence.result: 800 REML fit pairs (y vs y + 3.7A): maximum change in theta .00103 and in the REML criterion 1.7e-4; singular and warning flags identical in 799 of 800 fits each; the estimate shifted by exactly 3.7 (error 3e-14). Profiled ML: maximum deviance change 3e-5; singular flag identical in 798 of 800.

evidence.claim: Keeping a zero-variance focal slope is inference-neutral, so back-off gains power only by removing non-zero variances
evidence.result: 585 singular protected fits: median relative SE difference 3e-6 (max .026); Satterthwaite df 22.2 vs 22.2; rejection .59 vs .59.

evidence.claim: The lme4 documentation acknowledges no consensus and lists keep-maximal-until-non-singular, model selection and Bayesian or MAP options
evidence.result: Quotes: 'There is not yet consensus about how to deal with singularity'; 'singular models are statistically well defined'; default tolerance 1e-4.

evidence.claim: lme4 2.x adds structured covariances and recommends diag() over '||'
evidence.result: 2.0-1 (2026-03-05): cs(1 + f | g) and diag(...) added; '||' still splits terms by default (option lme4.doublevert.default = 'diag_special'); 'We recommend using diag(.) explicitly'. 2.1-0: ar1 and cs with zero variances return NA with a warning.

evidence.claim: glmmTMB offers heterogeneous and homogeneous compound symmetry
evidence.result: cs: n + 1 parameters; homcs: 2 parameters (equivalent to complex random intercepts apart from the sign constraint on rho).

evidence.claim: Existing reduction tools are data-driven and outcome-ordered
evidence.result: lmerTest::step: alpha.random = 0.1, then fixed-effect elimination at alpha.fixed = 0.05, reduce.fixed = TRUE by default. buildmer: direction c('order', 'backward'), LRT with Stram-Lee mixtures, singular.ok = FALSE, ddf = 'Wald' by default.

evidence.claim: Published practice orders reduction by estimated variance
evidence.result: afex: remove correlations, then the highest-order slopes estimated at zero; 'A model with a singular fit warning should not be reported or used'. RePsychLing (Bates et al.): maximal LMM, then zero-correlation, then drop the smallest variance components by LRT, then re-add correlations; the final model kept no by-subject slopes.

evidence.claim: Interaction tests need the highest-order within-unit slope
evidence.result: Type I error for the AB interaction with 4 and 8 replications: intercepts only .170 and .267; maximal .063 and .064; ANOVA .050 and .052. The guideline applies to simplifying non-converging models too.

evidence.claim: Maximal versus data-supported structures is the central disagreement
evidence.source: Barr et al. (2013), abstract; Matuschek et al. (2017), abstract plus a secondary summary
evidence.result: Barr: maximal models generalise best, and data-driven selection gives little or no power advantage. Matuschek: maximal models can cost substantial power, and selection (LRT, reportedly alpha .2, or AIC) does not inflate Type I error in their conditions. Exact simulation design not verified here.

evidence.claim: Omitting the lower-level slope in a cross-level interaction is severely anticonservative
evidence.result: Including the slope reduced |t| by 31% or more in three quarters of 30 ESS interactions (mean 42%); about half of the ESR cross-level estimates from 2011-2016 omitted the slope.

evidence.claim: Conflict: are level-1 slopes needed when the focal effect is at level 2?
evidence.source: Luo & Li (2023), abstract; Heisig, Schaeffer & Giesecke (2017), abstract summary
evidence.result: Luo and Li: not essential for cluster-level predictors, but control slopes increase power for within effects. Heisig et al.: ignoring varying control effects lowers the precision of context effects, especially with compositional differences and few clusters. Decision rule: ordering key k3 plus CR2 sensitivity analysis; HPC study H2.

evidence.claim: Complex random intercepts (CRIs) are a feasible intermediate structure
evidence.result: Excluding a within factor or interaction inflates Type I error; CRI models had low Type I error and more power in initial simulations; larger samples may favour random slopes.

evidence.claim: Conflict: is non-convergence evidence of over-parameterisation?
evidence.source: Bates et al. (2015), arXiv abstract; Eager & Roy (2017), arXiv abstract; Park et al. (2020), abstract
evidence.result: Bates: usually yes. Eager and Roy, with known non-zero variances: lme4 non-convergence 82% (complex logistic), 7% (simple logistic), 14% (complex linear); Stan near 0. Park: non-convergence rises sharply with complexity and removing correlations did not fix it. Decision rule: registry criteria with a second optimiser; HPC study H4.

evidence.claim: Selection by likelihood is biased or non-standard at the boundary
evidence.source: Greven & Kneib (2010); Self & Liang (1987); Stram & Lee (1994), abstracts
evidence.result: Marginal AIC is not asymptotically unbiased and favours models without random effects. LRT statistics for variance components follow chi-square mixtures, so naive chi-square tests are conservative.

evidence.claim: Bayesian testing does not escape the slope problem
evidence.source: Oberauer (2022); Verissimo (2023); van Doorn et al. (2023); Heck & Bockting (online 2021), abstracts
evidence.result: Omitting slopes gave strong Bayes factors for non-existent effects. Mismatched fixed and random parts inflate evidence. Experts disagreed on the null model. Model averaging propagates uncertainty about slopes.

evidence.claim: Few-cluster alternatives to dropping slopes exist, each changing the estimator or estimand
evidence.source: Oberpriller et al. (2022); Huang & Zhang (2025); Zhang & Lai (2024); Elff et al. (2021), abstracts
evidence.result: Fixed grouping after a singular fit avoided overconfidence. RI + CR2 approximates random-slope inference, though random-slope models have more power for level-2 and cross-level effects with few clusters. KR with random slopes was miscalibrated under level-2 heteroscedasticity while CR-SEs were not. REML with t and suitable df works for few clusters.

evidence.claim: Practice varies and analytic flexibility changes results
evidence.source: Meteyard & Davies (2020); Coretta et al. (2023); Roettger (2019), abstracts
evidence.result: Survey of 163 researchers and review of 400 papers showed no agreed standards; 46 teams produced substantially different effect sizes from the same data; exploring analytic choices inflates false positives.

evidence.claim: Blinding and preregistration support an outcome-blind default with logged unblinding
evidence.source: MacCoun & Perlmutter (2015); Dutilh et al. (2021); Sarafoglou et al. (2023), abstracts
evidence.result: Decisions are finalised before results are seen and later analyses are reported as post-blind. Blinding took about as long as preregistration across 120 teams, and blinded teams planned analyses they deviated from less.

evidence.claim: Deviations and prior knowledge should be reported in a structured way
evidence.source: Willroth & Atherton (2024); Lakens (2024); van den Akker et al. (2021); Roettger (2021), abstracts
evidence.result: Templates exist for reporting deviations and for prior knowledge of secondary data; a workshop slide deck says Roettger (2021) covers contingency plans for non-convergence (not read here).

evidence.claim: Fixed-effect tests after selection should use Satterthwaite or KR df
evidence.result: LRT and t-as-z were anticonservative in small samples; KR and Satterthwaite were acceptable.

recommendations.question: Q2 (version 1 model scope)
recommendations.decision: v1.0: Stream B audits cover every outcome type, in both languages with exact parity. The types are Gaussian, binary, binomial with trials, counts with exposure, bounded scores, ordinal items and positive durations. Checks are T0 from the codebook (type, event level, trials, exposure, bounds) and T1 from the data (constant clusters, minority events per cluster, boundary and zero shares). The engine-free separation LP for binary outcomes is a declared contingency, run with lpSolveAPI (LGPL-2, in Suggests) in R and scipy's default HiGHS solver in Python. Stream A diagnoses Gaussian LMMs only: lmerMod, lmerModLmerTest, afex mixed objects, glmmTMB gaussian, statsmodels MixedLM, and any engine key A promotes. For a single Likert item that is about to be modelled as metric, Stream B gives a T0 warning and states that Stream A cannot yet diagnose cumulative-link models.
recommendations.rationale: Usage. Gaussian LMMs dominate (Meteyard & Davies, 2020, reviewed 400 LMM papers; Luo et al., 2021, 301 multilevel articles; Dedrick et al., 2009, 99). Among GLMMs, binary outcomes dominate: in Bono et al. (2021), 50% of 118 analyses had nominal outcomes, and the family table lists binomial 19.5%, Poisson 9.3% and NB 2.5%. Binary outcomes are also standard in psycholinguistics (Jaeger, 2008) and L2 research (Linck & Cunnings, 2015). Ordinal items were analysed as metric in 100% of the relevant articles in three top journals (Liddell & Kruschke, 2018). A pre-fit warning is therefore worth more now than CLMM diagnostics. Engine-free audits cost little, need no fitting engine and can match exactly across languages, so they serve binary-accuracy users from v1.0. Stream A is held to Gaussian because statsmodels has no frequentist GLMM. GLMM support also costs more (next item).

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Drops cheap, exact-parity audits for binary and count outcomes (events per cluster, constant clusters, separation, exposure), which matter most for accuracy data
Roughly 8 times the validation compute per check, the hardest convergence triage, no Python parity, and a higher risk of two half-finished packages for one maintainer
More than 20 families, each needing its own contract fields (CDF, quantile, simulate, dispersion), residual type and validation grid

recommendations.revisit_if: A Python GLMM engine meets key A's promotion rule, the maintainer's own projects need binary GLMM diagnostics before v1.0, or a co-maintainer joins

recommendations.question: Q2 (roadmap after v1.0)
recommendations.decision: v1.1 adds Bernoulli, binomial-with-trials and Poisson GLMMs in R (glmer, glmmTMB). Python gets them only through an engine promoted by key A's rule, otherwise not_available. v1.2 adds negative binomial (NB1, NB2), beta, ordered beta, beta-binomial, Gamma and lognormal, all R only and with estimand labels. v1.3 adds structured covariance in R: glmmTMB ar1, ou, toep and cs, and lme4 >= 2.0-1 cs, diag and ar1, with semivariograms. v2 candidates, R only and started on demand: ordinal CLMMs (glmmTMB ordinal family or ordinal::clmm), zero-inflated and hurdle models, and an nlme adapter. Never in Stream A: Bayesian fits, GAMMs, multiple membership, nonlinear mixed models and multilevel SEM. Each report states where coverage ends, and Stream B still applies before fitting. A class is promoted only after its checks have HPC-validated false-flag and detection rates. Release table: q2_roadmap.csv.
recommendations.rationale: Need. GLMM reporting gaps are large: overdispersion was mentioned in 9.3% of analyses, covariance structure in 13.9%, and distribution or link went unstated in more than half (Bono et al., 2021). So GLMMs come in the first minor release, not later. Work. In easystats performance's NEWS, entries naming binomial, Poisson or GLMM (33), glmmTMB (23), dispersion (20) and zero inflation (14) far outnumber those naming lmer or lme4 (6). This is a crude keyword count. In a 1,600-row crossed design with maximal random effects, GLMM fits took 0.48 to 1.63 s against 0.17 s for lmer. A bootstrap-calibrated validation grid (24 cells, 1,000 replicates, 201 fits each) therefore costs about 920 to 2,200 CPU-h per GLMM family against about 230 for lmer. Drawing 250 simulations took 0.17 s or less, so refits dominate the cost. Bernoulli models warned in 15/30 (glmer) and 19/30 (glmmTMB) correctly specified datasets, against 5/30 for lmer and 0/30 for Poisson glmer, so convergence triage is the main work for binary GLMMs. Parity. glmm and mixedlm fit binomial, Poisson, NB and Gamma GLMMs but are young single-maintainer engines, and mixedlm's glmer_nb does not estimate theta. No Python frequentist engine fits ordinal, beta, zero-inflated, hurdle or residual AR(1) models. Everything after v1.1 is therefore R-only and must be labelled so. Bayesian diagnostics are already served by bayesplot, posterior, loo and ArviZ.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Different object model (no theta or Lambda), R-only, and no usage evidence that outweighs binary GLMMs
Separate diagnostic paradigm (R-hat, ESS, divergences, posterior predictive checks, LOO) with mature tools; Stream B already serves Bayesian users before fitting
Few users fit CLMMs today; the T0 warning gives most of the benefit at little cost

recommendations.revisit_if: The issue tracker shows different demand, the maintainer needs ordinal or AR(1) models for his own work, HPC validation shows a GLMM check cannot be calibrated (then ship it as descriptive only), or current lme4 2.1-0 and glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 give materially different warning rates from the versions tested here

recommendations.question: Q5 (report architecture and formats)
recommendations.decision: Canonical output: the results JSON, always written. Default human-readable output: one self-contained HTML file built from the shared logic-less template. It contains no scripts, makes no external requests and has a print stylesheet, so a browser's Save as PDF gives a PDF without other tools. Optional .qmd export: an engine-free Quarto Markdown folder with no code chunks. Values come from a generated metadata file through {{< meta >}} shortcodes, figures are SVG files with fig-alt, and the results JSON is included with its SHA-256. The user renders it with their own Quarto to html, docx, or PDF via Typst; pdf-standard: ua-1 requires Quarto 1.9 or later. The package never calls LaTeX and never depends on Quarto. In R, quarto (>= 1.5.0) stays in Suggests and the render helper is guarded with requireNamespace() and quarto_available(min = '1.9'). In Python, the CLI is found with shutil.which. Both packages also produce: a preregistration block (Markdown and hashed JSON) keyed to the OSF Preregistration and PRP-QUANT fields; methods text and APA-style tables generated only from the JSON, with mandatory elements and banned phrases; and an optional CSV of the long results table. No interactive plots in v1. Outputs and defaults: q5_report_outputs.csv; standards mapping: q5_standards_to_report_elements.csv.
recommendations.rationale: Journals and preregistration platforms want Word or PDF. Quarto bundles pandoc and Typst (1.10.20 and 1.11.9 ship pandoc 3.10 and Typst 0.15.1), so docx and PDF need no TeX. Quarto 1.9 added pdf-standard (PDF/UA, PDF/A) and passes alt text to Typst and LaTeX images, and it bundles Typst 0.14.2; Typst has tagged PDFs by default since 0.14. Pandoc's docx writer has carried image alt text since 1.17, and embedded SVG was fixed in 3.1.10. Chrome has tagged PDFs printed with Save as PDF since version 85. On CRAN, packages may write only to the temporary directory and must not start browsers in examples or tests (policy revision 6985). The quarto R package's own NEWS (1.5.1) records CRAN check failures on machines without Quarto. PyPI quarto-cli is an sdist that downloads Quarto at install time, so it cannot be a dependency. The OSF template asks for model specification detailed enough to rerun the analysis, coding schemes, inference criteria, exclusion and outlier rules, and units at each level, which is exactly what Stream B produces. JARS-Quant (data diagnostics), Meteyard & Davies, LEVEL and the CONSORT cluster extension (ICC per primary outcome) set the mandatory content. Report what was checked and what could not be assessed, never 'assumptions were met'.

alternatives_rejected.option: Direct PDF via LaTeX from the package
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Heavy system dependency absent from CRAN check machines; Quarto's default KOMA classes do not produce correctly tagged PDFs

alternatives_rejected.option: rmarkdown/knitr HTML in R and a separate Python renderer
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Needs pandoc, is R-only, and breaks report parity
Two more code paths with no parity gain; the .qmd route already gives Word with alt text
Not available on CRAN machines; the quarto package itself failed CRAN checks without the CLI

In my test, a plotly HTML file contained exact values (base64 float64) and all 300 IDs and loaded plotly.js from a CDN; custom widgets add keyboard, focus, target-size and name-role-value obligations under WCAG

recommendations.revisit_if: Users without Quarto need Word routinely, or journals in the target fields start accepting HTML supplements as the primary format

recommendations.question: Q5 (privacy defaults for participant-level and children's data)
recommendations.decision: Default privacy mode is 'shareable'. It shows no row-level values, IDs, minima, maxima, outliers or point plots, and every figure is aggregated. Each displayed cell, bin or band must contain at least k = 10 distinct data subjects. k counts persons, the declared disclosure unit, not rows. A dominance check applies: the two largest contributors must supply less than 90% of a bin's rows. Counts from 1 to 9 are shown as '<10', with margins rounded to base 5 so that suppressed cells cannot be recovered by differencing. Zeros in cross-tabs of person attributes are treated as disclosive. Outer bins are open-ended. Flagged clusters get report-local labels, and the label-to-ID mapping stays in memory only. Reports contain no paths, user names or host names. A banner says that shareable mode reduces disclosure risk but does not make the report anonymous data. 'internal' mode needs an explicit argument and carries a banner, contains_row_level_data: true and an _INTERNAL file suffix; its point-level figures are PNG. All parameters live in the registry and are recorded in the JSON. Rules: q5_privacy_and_accessibility_defaults.csv.
recommendations.rationale: The ONS Secure Research Service checks all outputs against a default low-count threshold of 10 under principles-based output checking, and DfE uses that default. That guidance treats scatter points as single data subjects, generally clears binned scatter graphs and generally does not permit outliers. The UK SDC Handbook v2.0 applies table principles to graphs and calls scatter plots generally disclosive. ACRO's defaults are threshold 10, residual df 10, dominance (2, 0.90), zeros disclosive and rounding base 5, and ACRO blocks .svg outputs and flags bin-edge disclosure. GDPR Recital 26 keeps pseudonymised data personal, the ICO's 2025 guidance uses a motivated-intruder test, and Recital 38 gives children specific protection. My experiment showed that an SVG scatter returned all 300 points exactly. A 4.3 KB, 100-dpi PNG returned the five most extreme residuals to within 0.26 units on an 80-unit axis. Rasterising is therefore not a protection.

alternatives_rejected.option: Raster point plots as the privacy measure
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Extreme values were recovered from a 100-dpi PNG to within 0.26 units

alternatives_rejected.option: Full detail by default with an opt-in redaction
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Reports get shared by default; the safe setting must be the default for children's data

alternatives_rejected.option: k = 5 or k counted on rows
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Below the UK trusted-research-environment default; with trial-level data, rows can all come from one person

recommendations.revisit_if: A data provider (for example DfE via the SRS, or the UK Data Service) sets other thresholds, the Oxford DPO advises otherwise, or HPC disclosure-attack tests show that combining figures reveals suppressed values

recommendations.question: Q5 (plot types and rendering)
recommendations.decision: Use static figures only. In shareable mode, draw a fixed set of aggregated plots as inline SVG. Coordinates are computed in the shared view model and written through the same logic-less templates as the HTML, so figures are byte-identical across languages and the core needs no plotting package. The set is: binned residual-vs-fitted quantile bands; normal quantile comparison at fixed probabilities against a simultaneous envelope band; standardised BLUP quantile bands; cluster-size and design-structure charts; the ceiling and ladder matrix; leave-one-cluster-out sensitivity bands; binned semivariograms; and, from v1.1, quantile-residual uniformity bands, binned residuals for binary outcomes and simulated dispersion and zero histograms. Native ggplot2 and matplotlib versions are offered only as optional plot() methods in Suggests or extras. Point-level versions appear only in internal mode, as PNG. Plot table: q5_plot_types.csv.
recommendations.rationale: Byte-identical SVG makes figure parity testable by hash, like the rest of the report. ggplot2 and matplotlib are optional, so a core report that drew natively would lose its figures when they are absent. Inline SVG can carry role='img', <title> and <desc>, keeps text as text when resized, and takes its contrast from the registry. Aggregated SVG contains only aggregated coordinates, whereas matplotlib's SVG writes one element per observation.

alternatives_rejected.option: Native ggplot2 and matplotlib for the report (as in the proposal)
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Two code paths, visual parity impossible, and the core report depends on optional packages
Dependency-free in R only, and still differs visually from Python

recommendations.revisit_if: Building the shared SVG layer proves costlier than two native plotting paths, or users insist on editable native figures in the report itself

recommendations.question: Q5 (accessibility)
recommendations.decision: Target WCAG 2.2 AA for the HTML report. Set lang and a page title, use a heading hierarchy, and give tables th, scope and captions. Every figure gets short alt text, a long description generated from the results and its aggregated data table. Status is shown by text and shape, never by colour alone. Essential marks use only blue #0072B2, vermillion #D55E00, bluish green #009E73, reddish purple #CC79A7 and black, on white panels. Orange, sky blue, yellow and grey are kept for non-essential fills with outlines. Body text has at least 4.5:1 contrast. Content reflows at 320 CSS px, with tables scrolling in their own containers, and supports 200% resize and text-spacing overrides. There are no custom widgets; <details> is allowed. In monorepo CI, golden reports pass an axe-core scan and an HTML validator, and a test render with Quarto Typst and pdf-standard: ua-1 passes Typst's own validation and veraPDF.
recommendations.rationale: I read the text of SC 1.1.1, 1.3.1, 1.4.1, 1.4.3, 1.4.4, 1.4.10, 1.4.11, 1.4.12, 2.1.1, 2.4.2, 2.4.11, 2.5.8, 3.1.1 and 4.1.2 from W3C's source. The Understanding note on 1.1.1 says a chart's long description should give the chart type, a summary and trends, and the data in a table where practical. The five chosen colours have at least 3:1 contrast against white (bluish green 3.42, blue 5.19, vermillion 3.87, reddish purple 3.06, black 21), and the four chromatic ones also against #121212. Orange (2.25), sky blue (2.31), yellow (1.32) and grey (2.85) fail against white. UK public-sector monitoring has tested against WCAG 2.2 AA since October 2024. Quarto bundles axe-core 4.10.3 and installs veraPDF.

alternatives_rejected.option: Use the full Okabe-Ito palette for essential marks
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Four of its eight colours fall below 3:1 against white
Fail SC 1.4.1 and invite certification creep

recommendations.revisit_if: WCAG 3 becomes the UK monitoring standard, or screen-reader testing shows the long descriptions are not usable
