recommendations.question: Q6-interop
recommendations.decision: Keep all diagnostic computation independent of easystats and DHARMa, and interoperate through Suggests only. No registry check takes its status, threshold or severity from performance, insight or DHARMa. When those packages are installed, the report may add clearly labelled R-only cross-check rows (for example performance::check_singularity(), check_convergence(), r2_nakagawa() and icc(), or DHARMa dispersion and uniformity tests). Each row records the package version and is excluded from parity claims. Results are exported as a plain long data frame that easystats and broom users can consume. Do not register methods on insight or performance generics unless the package later defines its own model classes. In that case insight's guide asks for support to be added upstream; delayed registration, S3method(insight::gen, cls), is the fallback.
recommendations.rationale: Install weight does not decide the easystats question, because performance, insight, datawizard and bayestestR are 4 pure-R packages. Four other things do. (1) Semantics: insight 1.7.0's is_converged.merMod, which performance::check_convergence() wraps, returns FALSE whenever lme4 skipped its derivatives, so 'not assessable' is reported as 'not converged'. icc() and r2_nakagawa() also make internal variance choices through insight::get_variance(). (2) Stability: insight had 22 CRAN releases in the last two years and performance 13, so delegated values could change without any registry version bump. (3) Parity: Python cannot call these functions, so every delegated quantity would become a permanent parity exception. (4) Licences: insight, performance and DHARMa are GPL-3 or GPL (>= 3), so their code can be called but not copied into an MIT package. DHARMa is ruled out as an import on cost alone: its hard closure is 94 packages, 49 of them compiled and non-recommended, including shiny and plotly pulled in through qgam and gap. On extension: insight's model-access functions and performance's check_singularity, check_collinearity, r2 and check_model are S3 generics. check_convergence and icc are not; they delegate to insight::is_converged and insight::get_variance. Of 45 sampled CRAN NAMESPACE files, none registers methods on these generics, which matches insight's guidance to add support upstream.

alternatives_rejected.option: Import performance or insight and delegate R2, ICC, VIF and convergence to them
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Convergence semantics conflict with a status taxonomy that separates 'not assessable' from 'fail'. Releases come almost monthly, and every delegated value becomes a Python parity exception.
94-package hard closure, 49 of them compiled and non-recommended, with shiny, plotly, httpuv, curl and openssl. Python has no equivalent, so it would sit outside parity.
Labelled cross-checks in Suggests cost little and let easystats users reconcile the two outputs.

recommendations.revisit_if: insight or performance distinguish 'not assessable' from FALSE and publish versioned definitions, or users ask for objects that performance can consume.

recommendations.question: Q6-lme4-and-split
recommendations.decision: Put lme4 in Suggests and do not split the package for now. Imports: Matrix (with no version floor above what R 4.2's bundled Matrix provides), jsonlite and base packages only (stats, utils, tools, methods, graphics, grDevices). Template rendering is either an in-house Mustache-subset renderer tested against the MIT-licensed Mustache spec or whisker in Imports, never in Suggests if the HTML report is core. Suggests: lme4, glmmTMB, lmerTest, pbkrtest, afex, performance, insight, DHARMa, ggplot2, quarto (>= 1.5.0) and testthat. Register diagnose() methods for merMod, glmmTMB and afex 'mixed' objects. Call engines as lme4:: inside requireNamespace() guards, and return 'not_available' with the missing package's name when a guard fails. Keep the package pure R, with no LinkingTo.
recommendations.rationale: The audit core's hard closure is 3 packages (Matrix, lattice, jsonlite). Adding lme4 makes it 14, 7 of them compiled and non-recommended (Rcpp, RcppEigen, minqa, nloptr, rbibutils, lme4, jsonlite), and nloptr needs cmake when no system nlopt is present. Adding glmmTMB makes it 65, lmerTest plus pbkrtest 61, and everything together 118. A hard closure's R floor can move without notice: Deriv 4.3.5 (2026-09-03) began requiring R >= 4.5, and through doBy and pbkrtest that now applies to glmmTMB, which declares R >= 3.6.0. Stream A loses nothing with lme4 in Suggests, because diagnose(fit) only receives objects made by an engine that is already installed. A demo package passed R CMD check with and without Suggests (_R_CHECK_DEPENDS_ONLY_=true). It dispatched lmerMod, glmerMod, lmerModLmerTest, afex mixed and glmmTMB objects without importing lme4, and library() loaded 4 namespaces instead of 12 (median 0.48 s against 0.64 s). Precedents: HLMdiag registers 15 or more lmerMod methods with lme4 in Suggests, and insight and performance also keep lme4 in Suggests. Writing R Extensions requires conditional use of anything in Suggests, recommended packages included, and recommends checking with _R_CHECK_DEPENDS_ONLY_ and _R_CHECK_SUGGESTS_ONLY_. For one maintainer, splitting into two packages would double CRAN submissions (the policy expects updates 'no more than every 1-2 months'), NEWS files and version coupling, while Suggests-gating already removes the install weight.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Every audit-only user would compile 7 packages from source on Linux or HPC, and the package would inherit future R-floor jumps in lme4's closure.
Doubles release and maintenance overhead for one maintainer for no install-weight gain over Suggests-gating.
Enhances packages cannot be required for checks. Suggests is the documented field for test-time and conditional use.

recommendations.revisit_if: A Stream A feature needs compiled linking to an engine, the ladder-fitting layer needs glmmTMB, pbkrtest or lmerTest as hard dependencies, or CRAN check-time limits are reached.

recommendations.question: Q7-name
recommendations.decision: Use one name in both languages: mixedcheck, as the CRAN package, the PyPI distribution and import package, and the conda-forge packages r-mixedcheck and mixedcheck. Rename the GitHub repository to match (GitHub redirects old URLs), or keep lmecheck as the repository name only. Second choice: lmecheck, if continuity matters more and the scope stays mainly Gaussian LMMs.
recommendations.rationale: All main candidates except mmcheck (taken on PyPI) are free on CRAN, Bioconductor, PyPI and conda-forge. The CRAN check covered current and archived packages, case-insensitively, through the cran mirror. The PyPI check covered exact names and Warehouse's 'too similar' rule. CRAN names are permanent ('in general it is not permitted to change a package's name'), so the name should fit the eventual scope, which the plan extends to GLMMs and glmmTMB. 'lme' and 'lmm' signal linear models only, and 'lme' also evokes nlme::lme, which is out of scope, and invites LME/LMM typos. 'diag' collides with lme4 2.x diag() covariance terms. 'mlm' is R's multivariate-lm class. 'glmm' suggests the unrelated glmm packages on CRAN and PyPI. 'audit' undersells Stream A and the reports. mixedcheck is short and lowercase, valid both as an R package name and as a PEP 8 import name, matches the common phrase 'mixed models' (afex::mixed), and avoids the mixture or MCMC connotation of 'mix'. Its drawback is search noise from the audio products 'MixChecker' and 'Mix Check Studio', which are in a different domain. Using the same name in R and Python follows marginaleffects, pins, vetiver, pointblank and duckdb. Do not upload a placeholder to PyPI: PEP 541 prohibits name squatting.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Linear only, and close to CRAN 'lmm'.
Taken on PyPI.
'diag' is ambiguous with lme4 2.x diag() covariance terms.
Suggest mixture models or MCMC mixing.
Easily mistaken for a companion to the unrelated CRAN or PyPI glmm packages.
Free, but 'audit' fits Stream B more than diagnostics and reporting.
'mlm' is R's multivariate linear model class.

recommendations.revisit_if: pak::pkg_name_check() or the R-universe search shows a conflict, the project is permanently limited to Gaussian LMMs (then lmecheck is fine), or Oxford requires different naming or branding.

recommendations.question: Q7-monorepo
recommendations.decision: Use one monorepo with r/ (R package root), python/ (pyproject root with src layout), spec/ (YAML source, JSON Schema and compiled JSON), fixtures/ (shared goldens plus a PROVENANCE file), parity/ (cross-language harness), sim/ (HPC validation code and SLURM templates, never shipped), paper/ (JOSS paper.md) and docs/. Commit byte-identical vendored copies of the compiled registry into r/inst/ and python/src/mixedcheck/, and have CI fail on any SHA-256 mismatch, so that no build step reaches outside a package directory. Use path-filtered CI workflows, an R-universe registry entry with "subdir": "r", and PyPI Trusted Publishing from python/ (pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish with packages-dir). Version the two packages independently, each recording the registry version it ships.
recommendations.rationale: CRAN and PyPI receive only built artefacts, so repository layout does not matter to them. Every install path supports subdirectories: remotes 'owner/repo/subdir', pak GitHub references with a subdirectory, pip '#subdirectory=' and R-universe 'subdir', which also runs a bootstrap.R before R CMD build. The large monorepos (apache/arrow r/ with python/, dmlc/xgboost R-package/ with python-package/, LightGBM) need sync-cpp, bootstrap.R or build-cran-package.sh only because they bundle C++ from elsewhere in the tree. A pure R and pure Python project avoids that if the vendored copies are committed. Separate repositories (marginaleffects, pins, vetiver, duckdb-r) suit separate teams and release cadences, but here they would add cross-repository synchronisation of the registry and fixtures for one maintainer. JOSS requires the paper to sit in the same repository as the software, after more than six months of public, iterative development.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Registry and fixture synchronisation across repositories would need bots or manual vendoring.

alternatives_rejected.option: Copy spec/ into the packages at build time
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Breaks install_github(subdir) and pip VCS installs; only R-universe's bootstrap.R would run it.
Not portable to Windows checkouts and not preserved in build tarballs.

recommendations.revisit_if: A co-maintainer takes over one language, or path-filtered CI becomes too slow.

recommendations.question: Q10-R
recommendations.decision: Depends: R (>= 4.2). CI runs Ubuntu R-devel, release, oldrel-1 and 4.2; Windows and macOS on release; one job without Suggests; and one job with the oldest lme4 the package claims to support. Raise the floor only when a dependency or feature needs it, keeping within the tidyverse five-version window (4.3 after R 4.7, expected in spring 2027).
recommendations.rationale: The current release is R 4.6.2 (2026-10-29), so the tidyverse and r-lib policy (current, devel and four previous versions) puts the floor at 4.2, the version arrow also uses. R 4.2.0 made UTF-8 the native encoding on Windows, which removes a class of cross-language string and ID parity failures. The core closure (Matrix, jsonlite) imposes no higher floor. The proposal's R >= 4.1 would add a version on which Stream A is effectively uninstallable: lme4 2.1-0 needs Matrix >= 1.5-0 headers, R 4.1.x bundles an older Matrix (Ubuntu 22.04 has R 4.1.2 with Matrix 1.4-0), and current Matrix needs R >= 4.4. Declared floors are not effective floors: lme4 2.1-0 says R >= 3.6 and glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 says R >= 3.6.0, but a current-source install of glmmTMB needs R >= 4.5 because of Deriv. Engine tests should therefore run on release and oldrel, and the floor job should test core features.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: No UTF-8 on Windows, Stream A cannot be tested with bundled Matrix, and it falls outside the tidyverse window.
Excludes users with no core need.

recommendations.revisit_if: ARC offers no R module of 4.2 or later and containers are unavailable (then run the simulations in a container rather than lowering the floor), or R 4.7 is released and a dependency needs 4.3.

recommendations.question: Q10-Python
recommendations.decision: requires-python = ">=3.11" at first release, with CI on 3.11 to 3.15. Set core dependency floors from SPEC 0 at release time: today numpy >= 2.3, scipy >= 1.15 (1.16 from 2027 Q1) and pandas >= 2.3 (3.0 from 2027 Q2). Test both the lowest-direct and the latest resolution. Drop 3.11 when it reaches end of life (about October 2027).
recommendations.rationale: Python 3.10 reached end of life on 2026-10-01 (PEP 619), and on 3.10 users are capped at numpy 2.2.6, scipy 1.15.3 and pandas 2.3.3. SPEC 0's numpy floor from 2026 Q4 (2.3) itself requires Python >= 3.11, as do pandas 3.0, scipy 1.16 and 1.17, and matplotlib 3.11. Current requires_python values: statsmodels 0.15.0 >= 3.10, pandas 3.1.1 >= 3.11, numpy 2.5.4 and scipy 1.18.1 >= 3.12. On 3.11 users get numpy 2.4.6 and scipy 1.17.1, both inside SPEC 0's support windows. SPEC 0's own Python rule would already drop 3.12 (2026 Q4), but 3.11 receives security fixes until about October 2027, and a pure-Python package gains little by excluding it. Precedents: pyarrow and lightgbm require >= 3.11, xgboost >= 3.12. While pandas 2.3 is supported, CI must cover both pandas 2.3 and 3.x, because pandas 3 infers a new 'str' dtype whose missing value is NaN. uv's documentation recommends lowest-direct test runs for libraries.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: End of life, and it caps users below SPEC 0's numpy floor.
Excludes a CPython version that still receives security fixes, for little gain.

recommendations.revisit_if: The first release slips past October 2027 (then use >= 3.12), or a needed numpy or scipy feature requires 3.12.

recommendations.question: Q10-licence
recommendations.decision: Keep MIT for both packages and for everything in the monorepo (registry, schema, simulated fixtures). For R: License: MIT + file LICENSE, where LICENSE holds only the YEAR and COPYRIGHT HOLDER lines and the full text sits in an .Rbuildignore'd LICENSE.md. For Python: license = "MIT" and license-files = ["LICENSE"] (PEP 639). Never copy or translate code from GPL or AGPL packages: re-implement from papers and documentation, and log the provenance of each algorithm. Third-party data may enter fixtures only under CC0 or CC BY with attribution, recorded in fixtures/PROVENANCE, and GPL-packaged datasets are never vendored into the Python package. Before the first public release, check Oxford's approval rule and name the legal copyright holder correctly.
recommendations.rationale: Running GPL-2, GPL-3, AGPL-3 or LGPL-3 dependencies is compatible with an MIT package under both readings of the licences. The R FAQ says the GPL 'only restricts distribution of R or of other programs containing code from R', and R Packages 2e holds that a package's licence need not be compatible with packages it merely calls. The FSF counts Expat/MIT as GPL-compatible, so even under its combined-work view an MIT package can be conveyed with GPL dependencies. I saw the FSF wording only through a mirror. AGPL-3 section 13 binds only modified versions of the AGPL program. CRAN practice agrees: 25 permissively licensed packages in the 171-package sample have GPL-family hard dependencies (datawizard imports insight; shiny and quarto import htmltools; later and plyr link Rcpp). CRAN even distributes combinations the FSF calls incompatible: lme4 imports both GPL-2-only minqa and GPL-3 reformulas, and AGPL-3 glmmTMB links GPL-2-only TMB. MIT also beats the alternatives here. Apache-2.0 conflicts with the GPL-2-only packages in the closure (minqa, TMB, numDeriv, HLMdiag) under the FSF view. A GPL licence would push the Python half outside the BSD and MIT norms of statsmodels, numpy, pandas and scipy. MIT is OSI-approved, listed in R's license.db and accepted by rOpenSci ('CRAN or OSI accepted license') and JOSS (OSI).

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Incompatible with GPL-2-only dependencies under the FSF view, and deters Python adoption.

alternatives_rejected.option: GPL (>= 2) for R and MIT for Python
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Two licences for one shared registry and fixture set.
The FSF treats it as incompatible with GPL-2-only code in the closure.
Needs extra licence notes in both packages for no gain.

recommendations.revisit_if: Oxford requires university copyright or a specific licence, or a module must be ported from GPL source (it would then have to be GPL and live in a separate package).

recommendations.question: Q4
recommendations.decision: Make declarations optional by default and required by mode. (1) Checks whose inputs the data fix exactly run from the data every time: label incidence (nested, crossed or partially crossed), within/between status, cluster sizes, rank and connectivity. (2) Checks that depend on things the data cannot reveal run only from a declaration. These are ID scope (reused local labels versus the same unit), the randomisation unit and blocking, the observation key, variable roles and their timing relative to assignment, focal estimands, dyad roles and the EEG reference. Without a declaration such a check reports 'not assessable' or 'ambiguous' and names the field to declare. It never guesses or silently recodes. (3) The schema enforces a minimal set in three situations: confirmatory goal, outcome-blind or preregistration export, and trial features. The set is units with id_scope for every nested_in, observation.key, variables (outcome and assigned) and estimands, plus assignment.unit for cluster_randomised, multisite, stepped_wedge and partially_nested. (4) Both languages get draft_design(), which writes a declaration pre-filled from inference, with each inferred entry marked as x-inferred. It counts as a declaration only after the user edits or accepts it, and its hash and timestamp go into provenance.
recommendations.rationale: The experiments show that the ambiguities that matter cannot be settled from data. Reused labels and genuine crossing give identical incidence (E-E01). Recovering them from the outcome is weak where it matters most, and the outcome is off limits in outcome-blind mode anyway. Inferring the randomisation unit fails after one miscoded row in 2,000 and always fails for stepped-wedge designs (E-E02). Inferring the observation key is circular, because continuous measures make rows unique (E-E03). Real teaching datasets carry these problems: in mlmRev::Exam, student IDs are local to school and 4 (school, student) pairs are duplicated (E-E03, E-E04). Every design tool reviewed takes structure as declared input and infers none of it: DeclareDesign/fabricatr, designr, faux, simr and mixedpower. randomizr checks declared nesting against data (E-E08 to E-E11). Requiring a declaration everywhere would block diagnose(fit) on models users have already fitted and quick exploratory use, and would add support load for a single maintainer. The fallback with 'inferred' wording follows the L7-22 verifier.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Blocks the main Stream A entry point (diagnose(fit) with no extra files) and exploratory use. Most exact structural audits need no declaration.
E1 to E3 show that inference fails exactly on scope, randomisation unit and keys. Silent wrong inferences are worse than 'not assessable'.

alternatives_rejected.option: Use the outcome to choose nested versus crossed
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It uses the outcome (T2) and is unreliable: correct in 19.5 to 82.5% of replicates when the label SD was 0.05 to 0.1.
Splits genuinely crossed or mobile units (catalogue L1-01, L7-01).

recommendations.revisit_if: Pilot users routinely skip declarations even in confirmatory work: then make the draft-and-accept step mandatory for preregistration export. Or a community standard for design semantics appears in Frictionless or Psych-DS: then map the declaration onto it.

recommendations.question: Q4-schema-format
recommendations.decision: Use one canonical JSON declaration per dataset, validated by a JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) vendored byte-identically in both packages. The draft is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lmecheck/76ff8921-f521-5c13-b469-59b514d4e510/scratchpad/r2/E/schema/design.schema.json. Its table block is a subset of Frictionless Table Schema v2: fields with type, categories and categoriesOrdered, missingValues including labelled sentinel codes, primaryKey and uniqueKeys. Frictionless tools can therefore read the CSV typing. Both readers apply the same strict rules: UTF-8 without BOM, NFC strings, duplicate keys rejected, null, NaN and Infinity rejected, and types coerced from the schema, never from the parser. The hash is SHA-256 of the RFC 8785 (JCS) canonical form. In the packages, validation consists of structural checks generated from the schema, so no V8 is needed in R and no rpds-py in Python. Full JSON Schema validation runs in monorepo CI and as an optional Python extra. YAML is accepted only for authoring: it is read with every scalar as a string, coerced by the schema and stored as JSON.
recommendations.rationale: A prototype showed identical SHA-256 hashes in R (jsonlite 1.8.8 plus a JCS serialiser of about 70 lines) and Python (json plus rfc8785 0.1.4) for 6 example declarations and an edge-case file (E-E05). It also showed identical parsed-table hashes for all 10 fixtures, using read.csv in R and pandas in Python driven by the declared types (E-E07). Three hazards would break parity without explicit rules. jsonlite keeps duplicate keys while Python keeps the last one. jsonlite returns named list() for {} and list() for []. In a C locale R printed <U+00FC> escapes and needed a hand-written shortest round-trip float formatter. YAML typing diverges between R yaml 2.3.8 and PyYAML 6.0.3 for y/n, 1_000, 1,000, 12:30 and dates. Both parsers turn NO into false, 007 into 7 and 2026.10 into 2026.1 (E-E06). Frictionless v2 already covers typing, level order, labelled missing values and keys (E-E12), but R frictionless 2.0.x does not yet support categories (E-E13). The JSON Schema validators carry heavy dependencies: V8/libv8 in R, rpds-py in Python (E-E20).

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Parser divergences (E-E06) and YAML 1.1 coercions damage IDs and labels.

alternatives_rejected.option: A full Frictionless Data Package as the container, read with the frictionless packages
alternatives_rejected.why_not: It carries no design semantics. R frictionless imports dplyr, readr and httr and lacks categories support. A Data Package profile remains an optional export.
XML/RDF formats built for survey archives, with no lightweight readers in both languages; they contribute only a vocabulary (identifier, measure, attribute, dimension).
R code or R-specific JSON, not a language-neutral file that is checked against data.
Cannot express combinations such as a longitudinal multisite cluster RCT (L7-22 verifier). Compositional feature tags with conditional requirements replace it.

recommendations.revisit_if: R frictionless adds categories and fieldsMatch support, in which case consider shipping the declaration as a Data Package profile. Or a dependency-light JSON Schema validator becomes available in R.

recommendations.question: Q4-schema-vocabulary
recommendations.decision: Adopt draft vocabulary 0.1.0 with these blocks: schema_version (the only required field), goal, features (non-exclusive tags), table, units (name, columns, nested_in, id_scope, membership, role), crossings (with an optional list column), observation (unit, key, time with kind, within, ISO 8601 resolution and IANA time zone), assignment (column, unit, randomised, blocks, scheme, control_level, time_varying), variables (role, derived_from, bounds, measurement), estimands (id, term, kind, focal), dyad, eeg, imputation, provenance (created, author, outcome_seen attestation, data hash) and x-* extensions. Unknown keys are errors, so a misspelt nested_in cannot be silently ignored. The behaviour when each field is missing is listed in tables/q4_declaration_fields.csv.
recommendations.rationale: Each field maps onto a catalogue check or a reporting item. These include L1-01/L7-01 (id_scope), L7-03 and CONSORT cluster items 3a/7a/12a (assignment.unit, blocks), L1-15/L7-19 (key), L7-11/L7-12 (time zone and resolution), the critic gap on roles, L7-08 (dyad), L7-17 (eeg) and the multiple-imputation gap. The 6 examples validate. All 7 invalid files are rejected with specific messages, among them nested_in without id_scope, a typo key, and confirmatory goal without estimands.

alternatives_rejected.option: Roles stored as custom properties inside Frictionless field descriptors
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Allowed by the spec, but it mixes typing with design semantics, and a future Frictionless property could collide with it. A separate variables block keeps the table block a pure Frictionless subset.

recommendations.revisit_if: Writing the first domain vignettes shows a missing field, for example a sampling-weights level or plausible-value sets.

recommendations.question: Q8-domains
recommendations.decision: Let two designs drive defaults, message wording and the first two vignettes. The first is nested education data, including cluster-randomised and multisite trials. The second is crossed subjects x items with trial-level RT and binary accuracy. Longitudinal and intensive longitudinal data, including app logs, come in v0.2 as examples and checks. Families and dyads follow as a domain module in v0.2 to v0.3, fixtures first. Single-trial EEG comes later and stays in the monorepo. Defaults stay design-agnostic: domain checks and wording switch on from declared features, or from data patterns with 'inferred' wording.
recommendations.rationale: These two designs match the maintainer's fields (education now, psycholinguistics before). They span nesting versus crossing and Gaussian versus binary outcomes, and between them they exercise most Stream B checks: label scope, randomisation level, few clusters, design df, connectivity, one observation per cell and counterbalancing. Public data are plentiful for both, and several sets are reachable from Python through Rdatasets (E-E14, E-E15). Intensive longitudinal checks first need time-zone and lag infrastructure, and open ESM data are fetched from Zenodo. For dyads no well-licensed couples dataset was found. EEG data are large and CC BY-SA (E-E16).

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Needs declared time, time-zone and lag machinery before anything else, and the open data are only fetched at run time, so it is not CRAN-safe for examples.
Large data, MNE dependency, ShareAlike licence, reference-scheme subtleties.
They do not exercise the checks that set the suite apart, such as scope, randomisation unit and keys.

recommendations.revisit_if: Early users turn out to be mainly ILD or app-log researchers, or the maintainer's own app-log data become usable for validation.

recommendations.question: Q8-corpus
recommendations.decision: Use both simulated and public data, in four layers. (1) The simulated pathology zoo: tiny stored instances, MIT/CC0, bundled in both packages for layer-1 golden tests (10 prototype fixtures take 67 KB of CSV). Expectations are derived from the generating design, not from the suite, and the same generators drive the HPC validation. (2) Public datasets from R packages (lme4, nlme, mlmRev, languageR, afex, HistData, mixor). R uses them in examples and vignettes through Suggests with requireNamespace guards. The monorepo materialises them at CI time for cross-language parity tests without committing them. Python documentation fetches them at run time (statsmodels get_rdataset from Rdatasets, or openesm). Neither the CRAN tarball nor the PyPI wheel redistributes them. (3) Openly licensed external data (CC0 or CC BY, plus a CC BY-SA derivative of ERP CORE) go in a separate monorepo corpus folder with per-dataset licence and attribution files, added only after a local licence check. (4) The maintainer's restricted data serve private validation on ARC only and are never committed.
recommendations.rationale: The Rdatasets maintainer states that the licences of the data themselves could not be determined (E-E15), and the packages are GPL, AGPL (eefAnalytics) or Apache (OpenMx). Copying their data into an MIT wheel therefore adds licence risk for no gain. CRAN requires clear copyright for all components and graceful failure of Internet resources, and caps data at 5 MB as a general rule (E-E18). PyPI does not vet licences, so the responsibility falls on the project (E-E19). ERP CORE's ShareAlike terms require any derivative to carry the same licence (E-E16). Public data catch messiness that simulation misses: Exam's local IDs and duplicate keys, star's mobility, ScotsSec's cross-classification and guImmun's 1,063 singleton families (E-E04). Simulated fixtures give known answers and identical parsing in both languages (E-E07).

alternatives_rejected.why_not: Misses real artefacts such as local IDs and duplicate keys (E-E03, E-E04), and the reports need realistic vignettes.

alternatives_rejected.option: Bundle public datasets inside both packages
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Data licences are undetermined, it costs size, and it puts GPL/AGPL material in an MIT wheel.
CRAN checks must not depend on the network, and the tests would be flaky.

recommendations.revisit_if: A small education CRT dataset is confirmed as CC0 or CC BY (for example OSF 4p8hz). It could then be bundled in both packages with attribution as a realistic layer-1 fixture.

recommendations.question: Q8-zoo
recommendations.decision: Adopt the 30-fixture pathology zoo in tables/q8_pathology_zoo.csv, starting from the 10 prototyped fixtures: Z01 with its matched negative, Z02, Z04, Z07, Z08, Z09, Z11, Z13 and Z17. Each fixture has a seeded generator with its parameters, a tiny stored instance, a matched negative, a declaration whose table block types the CSV, the preliminary formula, by-construction expected findings with catalogue item links and a tier (T0/T1/T2), and a data hash. On ARC the same generators produce grids over J, n_j, imbalance and family, to estimate each check's false-flag rate under the matched negative and its detection rate under the planted problem. Results go to /data/educ-intract/educ1242/.
recommendations.rationale: An independent R recomputation reproduced all 11 by-construction quantities. Parsed-table hashes agree between R and Python for all 10 fixtures (E-E07). Every catalogue item that needs a positive and a negative case (L6-10) is covered, and the completeness critic's call for validation simulations is met.

alternatives_rejected.option: Goldens produced by running the suite itself
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Risks approving existing bugs (L6-10 verifier). By-construction expectations are independent anchors.

recommendations.revisit_if: The validation runs show a check with an uncontrolled false-flag rate. Its fixture grid then needs refinement before the threshold ships.

evidence.claim: Outcome-free data cannot distinguish reused class labels (true nesting) from genuine crossing, and the outcome distinguishes them reliably only when the label variance is large
evidence.result: Identical incidence by construction (4 labels in all 20 schools, fill rate 1). The ML log-likelihood picked the true structure in 19.5 to 82.5% of replicates (ties 2.5 to 42%) at label SD 0.05 to 0.1, in 54.5 to 99.5% at SD 0.2, and in 96 to 100% at SD 0.4 with 20 schools (school SD 0.4, residual SD 1, 200 replicates per cell, lme4 1.1-35.1)

evidence.claim: Inferring the randomisation unit as the coarsest level with constant treatment is brittle
evidence.result: School-randomised CRT (1,200 rows): correct 100% with no errors, 54.7% with 0.05% miscoded rows, 0.2% with 0.5%. Stepped wedge: 0%. Individual randomisation in 10 mostly singleton families: wrongly inferred as family-level 8.2%. Unblocked class randomisation: at least 99.9% correct (2,000 replicates)

evidence.claim: Inferring the observation key is circular, and a teaching dataset has local IDs and duplicate keys
evidence.result: sleepstudy: Reaction alone is a minimal key. fhch2010: (id, item) is a key. Exam: every minimal key contains a score column; (school, student) has 4 duplicated pairs (8 rows), one pair of different sex; 322 of 650 student labels occur in more than one school

evidence.claim: Public R datasets carry the structural pathologies the suite targets
evidence.result: ScotsSec: 61.5% of primaries feed more than one secondary (1 component). star: class type constant in all 1,387 teacher x grade cells, 3.85% of students change school, 62.8% have more than one teacher. guImmun: 1,063 of 1,595 families are singletons. recommendations.question: Q9-venue (software-plus-validation paper and a separate methods paper)
recommendations.decision: Two papers. (1) A preregistered methods paper on the validation study, sent first to Psychological Methods and then to Behavior Research Methods. Choose BRM first if the paper reads mainly as 'tool plus its validation' rather than as general findings about LMM diagnostics. (2) A JOSS software paper covering both packages from the monorepo, submitted once JOSS's gates are met, disclosing paper 1. Make the repository public now, because JOSS requires more than 6 months of public, iterative development history plus evidence of research use. Possible extra: an AMPPS tutorial. Single-paper alternative: JSS, if one long software-plus-validation paper and a review of about a year are acceptable. In that case skip JOSS.
recommendations.rationale: JOSS (verified from its GitHub docs): no fees. Desk-rejection gates: more than 6 months of public history, demonstrated research use, good open-source practice (relaxed for solo projects but needing several signals: releases, tests and CI, CONTRIBUTING, governance) and iterative development. Paper of 750–1,750 words with required State of the field, Software design, Research impact and AI-usage sections. Co-publication with a methods paper is allowed if disclosed. The paper must not focus on research results, so the validation study needs its own outlet. The R Journal (verified): R-only, package must be on CRAN, maturity-based desk rejections, median time to acceptance under a year. A poor fit for the dual-language parity story. JSS (search summaries of official pages): CC BY, no fees per DOAJ, replication materials plus a light script for a regular PC, GPL-compatible code (MIT qualifies), roughly 12–15 months to publication. Strong fit but slow. BRM: best audience fit (TOP Level 2, tutorials), hybrid OA probably covered by the Springer Nature–Jisc 2026–2028 agreement (Oxford participation unconfirmed), median 223 days to acceptance per a PubMed-derived aggregator. Psychological Methods: its scope explicitly covers methods for analysing psychological data and reviews of statistical software. Best home for generalisable operating characteristics. AMPPS: fully OA with a conflicting APC (USD 1,000 vs 1,500). JORS: charges an APC and duplicates JOSS. Full table: tables/venues.csv.

alternatives_rejected.option: R Journal for the software paper
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Must be primarily about R (the Python package is out of scope), requires maturity on CRAN, and gives no advantage over JOSS for one maintainer

alternatives_rejected.option: Both JOSS and JSS for the same software
alternatives_rejected.why_not: JSS policy on software already published in JOSS could not be read on the official site (host blocked). Treat it as a duplication risk
Same function as JOSS, but with an APC of uncertain size and low visibility in psychology and education
JOSS papers must not focus on new research results, so the validation would get no peer-reviewed home

recommendations.revisit_if: The JSS official pages show it accepts JOSS-published software, or Oxford is not covered by the Springer Nature or APA Jisc agreements, or the validation finds little beyond confirming existing tools (then JSS or BRM single paper)

recommendations.question: Q9-protocol (simulation validation of each check)
recommendations.decision: Validate the checks as 11 studies in ADEMP form (tables/validation_protocol.csv). V0 covers deterministic audits, validated by known-answer fixtures and property tests in CI (no HPC). V1 is a Gaussian null bank (306 cells × 2,000 replicates) on which every check runs, giving false-flag rates and family-wise flag counts. V2 is 13 targeted misspecification modules at 3 magnitudes × 8 representative cells × 1,000 replicates, giving detection rate, consequence for focal estimands, a cross-talk matrix and an action-value contrast ('switch to the registry alternative when flagged' vs never vs always). V3 covers singularity, convergence and boundary criteria; V4 variance-component tests and parametric bootstrap; V5 the reduction ladder (sibling key B's H1/H2/H5, with 2×2 cells capped at 1,536 rows); V6 calibration of outcome-blind design analysis; V7 cross-language parity. V8–V10 are the GLMM counterparts for v1.1. Pre-specified rules: a check is calibrated in a cell if the upper 95% Monte Carlo limit of its false-flag rate is at most .075 (test-based checks at alpha .05) or at most .05 (descriptive flags graded consequential). Assessability is adequate if detection is at least .80 at the smallest harmful magnitude, weak at .50–.80 and not assessable below .50. Harm means coverage below .925, Type I error above .075 or relative bias above 10% for a focal estimand. Tune thresholds only on a calibration half and confirm on the held-out half. Monte Carlo SE targets: .0049 for rates near .05 and for coverage (2,000 reps); at most .016 for detection and power (1,000 reps). Report non-convergence and failures as outcomes, never drop them. Preregister on OSF with the ADEMP-PreReg template after a pilot. Declare the study non-neutral and include comparators (performance::check_*, DHARMa, engine-native flags, naive variants) in default configuration.
recommendations.rationale: ADEMP and Monte Carlo SE formulas follow Morris et al. (2019) and the ADEMP-PreReg template of Siepe et al. (2024). Failure handling follows Pawel et al. (2026). Known-answer settings and staged coding follow White et al. (2024). Pawel et al. (2024) show how unregistered simulation designs can make any method look superior. Boulesteix et al. (2013) define why developer-run comparisons are not neutral. Shamsudheen & Hennig (2023) justify judging a diagnostic by the performance of the whole check-then-act procedure, not by its power alone. Sharing replicates across checks is the main efficiency: each dataset is fitted once and all checks run on that fit, so cost scales with fits, not checks. My pilot of the pipeline (2,000 lmer fits) shows why validation is needed. With J = 10 and m = 5 under a correct model with slope SD .15, lme4 flagged singularity in 64–69% of datasets (36–44% at J = 40), and a unit-free rank criterion agreed closely. A naive Bartlett test on raw conditional residuals stayed near nominal (.036–.062, MCSE about .01), so catalogue item L5-03's predicted inflation needs more extreme cells before it enters the registry. For one maintainer, build modules M06 (omitted slope), M10 (CRT randomisation level), M05, M01/M09, M04, M07 and M12 first; M02, M03, M08, M11 and M13 second.

alternatives_rejected.option: Full factorial over all design factors for every check
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Thousands of cells. Use the shared null bank plus representative cells per module, with fractional or Latin-hypercube grids and metamodels where needed (Skrondal 2000)

alternatives_rejected.option: Validating checks only by their detection power
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Ignores false flags, the consequences for focal estimands and the pre-test problem; the registry's assessability and consequence fields need all three

alternatives_rejected.option: Tuning thresholds on the same replicates used to report performance
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Overfits; requires a calibration/validation split

alternatives_rejected.option: Bootstrap-refit calibration for every GLMM check (key C's 201 fits per replicate)
alternatives_rejected.why_not: Multiplies cost by about 100. Validate simulate-without-refit versions and confine refit-based tests to V4/V10

recommendations.revisit_if: The pilot shows that the middle magnitudes produce no harm (re-choose them), that suite check code costs much more than one fit per replicate, or that catalogue predictions such as L5-03 fail in extreme cells

recommendations.question: Q9-hpc (compute budget and ARC plan)
recommendations.decision: Budget about 1,160 CPU-hours (central; range 700–2,300) for Phase 1 Gaussian LMMs (v1.0) and about 270 (160–540) for Phase 2 GLMMs (v1.1), roughly 1,430 in total. Run each study as a SLURM job array on htc's short partition (12 h limit, highest priority): 1 core and 2 GB per task, --constraint='cpu_gen:Cascade_Lake', BLAS threads pinned to 1, tasks packed to about 2–4 hours (requests of 4–9 hours), at most 500 tasks per array and a throttle of 200. The array sizes are in budget/array_plan.csv. Each chunk uses an L'Ecuyer-CMRG stream and each replicate a substream, so any dataset can be regenerated. Chunks are idempotent and written to $SCRATCH, then rsynced to /data/educ-intract/educ1242/lmecheck-sim/results. Store raw replicate-level results (about 2 million rows, a few GB). Mirror them off ARC, which keeps no backups and only two weeks of snapshots. Start with the HPC-0 calibration pilot. Use the tested base-R driver in slurm/ or SimDesign 2.28's runArraySimulation()/genSeeds().
recommendations.rationale: Timing ran on this VM: 4 cores, reference BLAS, lme4 1.1-35.1, glmmTMB 1.1.8, about 4.8 min of R plus 19 s of Python. Per-fit times: nested lmer 0.02–0.13 s (43–5,251 rows), glmer Bernoulli 0.07–0.84 s, glmmTMB 0.12–0.69 s. Crossed one-factor maximal fits: lmer 0.09/0.31/1.76 s and glmer 0.34/0.98/8.4 s at 384/1,536/6,144 rows. Crossed 2×2 maximal fits at 384/1,536 rows: lmer 0.72/4.1 s, glmmTMB Bernoulli 1.3/11.4 s, glmer Bernoulli 11/45 s. statsmodels crossed variance components: 0.95 s at 1,536 rows, 16.7 s at 6,144. Four concurrent processes slowed each job ×1.38. I fitted power laws per design and engine and composed per-replicate costs (focal fit, ML refit, alternative model, Satterthwaite, simulate(250), suite checks assumed equal to one fit). The multipliers are 1.38 for contention, 1.15 for reruns and 1.10 for the pilot, with ×0.6/×2 bands for node speed and versions. Key B's H1 ladder grid dominates. Uncapped, it costs about 1,430 CPU-hours alone (B estimated 200, assuming 0.07 s fits). Capping 2×2 cells at 1,536 rows cuts it to about 660. ARC facts from the user-guide sources on GitHub (oxford-arc): htc short partition with 124 nodes and 7,872 cores; medium 48 h; long 30 days per the scheduling page but 'unlimited' per the systems page; devel 10 min. Jobs default to 1 core and 8,000 MB per CPU. $DATA has 5 TiB shared, $HOME 15 GiB. Per-job $SCRATCH and $TMPDIR are deleted at job exit. Compute credit is checked with mybalance. R is provided as module R/4.4.0-gfbf-2023a. Apptainer images must be built off-cluster. Search summaries of arc.ox.ac.uk add that Social Sciences Division projects get standard credits under the free service, new projects receive 25,000 free core-hours, and the full economic cost is £0.01 per core-hour. The whole programme therefore fits a free allocation.

alternatives_rejected.why_not: About 2 million tiny jobs would overwhelm the scheduler and fair share; R start-up would dominate run time
htc favours small jobs. Single-core array tasks need no BLAS or thread tuning and keep replicates independent
Lower priority, and no task needs more than 12 hours once chunked
Doubles total Phase 1 cost for 2×2 cells at up to 6,144 rows, where each maximal lmer fit takes about 23 s

recommendations.revisit_if: HPC-0 calibration shows ARC per-fit times more than 1.5× those measured here, current lme4 2.1-0 changes fit times materially, or ARC limits (MaxArraySize, QoS) differ from SLURM defaults

recommendations.question: Q9-scope (one maintainer)
recommendations.decision: Tie the validation to releases. v0.x needs only V0 (CI). v1.0 needs V1, V2 (priority modules), V3, V5 (capped, shared with key B) and V7; V4 and V6 can follow. v1.1 needs V8–V10. The methods paper reports Phase 1. Defer B's H4, H8 and H10 (about 700 CPU-hours by B's estimates) unless reviewers ask. Indicative timeline: months 0–3 build the simulation package, pilot and preregistration; months 3–6 Phase 1 runs and v1.0; months 6–9 write and submit the methods paper, then JOSS once the 6-month history and research-use gates are met; months 9–15 Phase 2.
recommendations.rationale: Compute is not the binding constraint: about 1,430 CPU-hours is a few days on htc and costs nothing under a free allocation. Maintainer time for building data-generating mechanisms, the analysis and writing is. Reusing one null bank across all checks and prioritising education-relevant modules keeps the work proportionate.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q3.1 Single recommended formula, or ceiling + identifiability verdict + pre-specified ladder?
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The decision follows from sources I re-read in current CRAN master. lme4's man/isSingular.Rd says there is 'not yet consensus' and lists five strategies. afex (vignette), RePsychLing (KB.Rmd), lmerTest::step (3.2-1) and buildmer (2.13) each implement a different, outcome-ordered procedure. Every Sim 1 number quoted is exact: I recomputed all cells from the raw replicate files, and the original and rerun files agree on all 51,800 shared rows (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lmecheck/76ff8921-f521-5c13-b469-59b514d4e510/scratchpad/r2/B-verify/out/v1_recompute_sim1.txt). Two corrections. The maximal model's power deficit to the selection rules at tau <= .2 is 5.5-9.0 points, not 5-8. These power comparisons are not size-adjusted: the rules with more power also had higher realised Type I error. The survey and many-analyst figures (Meteyard & Davies; Coretta et al.) could not be checked here.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Keep the plan object. State in both the plan and the report that the operating characteristics of 'rule R on ladder L' are known only for the simulated cells until H1 has run.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q3.2 Ladder ordering
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The protected set is supported. Recomputed Sim 3: dropping the focal slope gave .226/.187, dropping the nuisance slope .054/.035. Recomputed Sim 2 agrees. Freezing coding before removing correlations is supported by Sim 4 and by lme4's getDoublevertDefault.Rd and glmmTMB's covstruct vignette. Weak points: (1) B-E04 does not show that outcome-free ordering costs little. The two slope SDs were equal, the paired rejection difference was at most .003 with at most 1% of data sets discordant, and both slopes are focal, so this ladder would protect them anyway. (2) Compound symmetry is coding-invariant only on cell indicators: cs(0+f|g), homcs or complex random intercepts (CRI). cs(1+f|g) over contrast columns depends on coding. lme4 2.x cs() is heterogeneous by default (hom = FALSE). CRI equals homcs only when rho >= 0, and statsmodels can express only CRI. (3) Ordering key k3 rests on content not verifiable here (Verissimo 2023; Luo & Li 2023) and on Sim 3, where dropping a correlated nuisance slope cost power but never inflated focal Type I error. (4) buildmer's include= already keeps user-named terms in the model, so a protected set is not new.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Keep the protected set, the coding and centring freeze, and correlations before variances. Specify the factor step as us -> cs(0+f|g) -> homcs or CRI, stating the sign constraint and which engines support each rung. Treat k3 and the order among nuisance terms as hypotheses for H2, tested with asymmetric slope variances. Drop the claim in B-E04.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q3.3 Default stopping rule and how to preregister it
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The rule needs substantial fixes. (1) As written ('accept an unprotected rung only if ... no random-effects covariance block is rank-deficient'), SR-P steps past every unprotected rung whenever a PROTECTED slope is at zero. It then strips non-zero nuisance slopes, the same mechanism the report blames for SR-U's extra power. My simulation v2 used 30 units of 20, a nuisance slope SD of .3 and the ladder us -> diag -> protected (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lmecheck/76ff8921-f521-5c13-b469-59b514d4e510/scratchpad/r2/B-verify/out/v2_summary_all.txt). SR-P as specified removed the nuisance slope in 40-45% of data sets when the focal slope SD was 0, and in 20-24% when it was .1. With the nuisance predictor correlated with the focal one (r = .5), this cost 2.6 power points (.796 vs .822, MCSE .56) and 1.8 points against a localised SR-P. With a nuisance SD of .5, the focal SE rose from .054 to .058 and Type I error fell to .029. (2) LRT(.2) and AIC were rejected on the evidence of their unprotected versions; Sims 1 and 2 contained no unprotected slopes at all. In v2, localised SR-P, protected LRT(.2) and protected AIC differed by at most .005 in all 14 cells, and Type I error for these rules and the ceiling ranged .032-.061. The evidence therefore supports the protected set, not one particular stopping rule. (3) Minor numerical errors: SR-U's gain is 4.0-4.7 points, not 4-7. The cost of protection reaches 7.8 points against AIC in the small design, and is 1.4-2.8 points in the large design, not 'about 1'. (4) The switching rule ignores multiplicity. With 2,000 replicates, a rule whose true rate is .05 exceeds .06 in a single cell with probability .020, and in at least one of 50 cells with probability .63 (out/v3_cost_and_multiplicity.txt). In v2 the ceiling itself reached .061. (5) In glmmTMB a singular protected rung often has a non-positive-definite Hessian with NA standard errors (catalogue L4-05), so SR-P is engine-dependent exactly at the protected rung.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Localise the criterion: step down only on non-convergence, or when the boundary direction lies in unprotected parameters. An alternative is to remove exactly the zero-variance unprotected directions, which was inference-neutral in about 98% of fits in Sim 6. Accept boundary directions confined to protected terms. Describe the choice between SR-P and protected LRT(.2) as a value judgement to be settled by H1, not as an evidence-based default. Make the switching rule metamodel- or confidence-bound-based and relative to the ceiling or an oracle model. Specify how a singular protected rung is handled in glmmTMB: fix the variance at zero through map, or drop the zero direction.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q3.4 Outcome-blind default; unlocking and logging T1/T2
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: T0 as the default is consistent with the proposal, and the invariance for Gaussian LMMs holds. I recomputed Sim 5: singular flags identical in 799/800 REML fits, warnings in 799/800, ML singular flags in 798/800. The REML and profiled-ML algebra implies the same. But because selection is invariant to the focal fixed effect, masking cannot change any decision of an automated rule. It only keeps the focal estimate from the analyst, so it is an attestation, and managing a secret adds work without adding protection. A hash-chained append-only log cannot stop the person who controls the files from rewriting it; a third-party timestamp, such as an OSF or Zenodo deposit, is what makes a plan credible. The claims attributed to Sarafoglou et al. (2023) and Dutilh et al. (2021) could not be checked here.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Keep T0 as the default, and keep unlocking T1 against a frozen plan hash. Replace the hash chain with a plain JSON log that records the plan hash and tier, and recommend depositing the plan with a third party. Implement masking as a two-step API: select and freeze the rung, then fit and reveal the estimates. No secret is needed. Defer masking for GLMMs.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q3.5 Unsettled questions needing HPC simulation
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The H1-H10 structure, the ADEMP framework and the replicate counts are reasonable. Five problems. (1) H1 omits the comparisons that decide the default: localised versus global SR-P, and protected versus unprotected LRT and AIC (see v2). (2) The CPU budget excludes Kenward-Roger df and the parametric bootstrap, although both are listed as factors. KR took 21 s per fit at n = 1,536 against 0.2 s for the fit. A bootstrap LRT took about 0.17 s per draw, roughly 95 CPU-hours per cell at 1,000 draws x 2,000 replicates (v3, timed under load). (3) The decision rule has no multiplicity control (see Q3.3). (4) The claim that no published simulation tests back-off on singular fits conflicts with the report's own extraction of Oberpriller et al. (2022), who simulated switching to fixed grouping after a singular fit, and of Scandola & Tidoni's (2024) simulation-validated step-by-step procedure (content unverified here). (5) Engine versions must be pinned: lme4 2.1-0 changed glmer's PIRLS step, which changes GLMM standard errors (NEWS verified).
recommendation_verdicts.change: Add the localised and protected variants to H1, and asymmetric slope variances plus failure-based rules to H2. Restrict KR and the parametric bootstrap to the smallest cells or to a subsample of replicates. Preregister a metamodel-based decision rule with multiplicity control. Pin and report the versions of lme4, glmmTMB and lmerTest; the current lmerTest is 3.2-1, against 3.1-3 used here.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q3.6 Scope for one maintainer and the paper
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: Deferring the Bayesian and averaging alternatives and masking for GLMMs is right. Release 1 still carries three heavy items. The first is the suite's own scaled gradient and Hessian checks with a second optimiser, in two languages. It is required because lme4 >= 1.1-38 skips derivative checks for singular fits, large n and many parameters (NEWS verified), and it is costly for maximal models and has to be built separately for statsmodels. The other two are hash-chained logs and masked execution with secret handling. The paper plan includes H4 (GLMMs, the costliest study), although GLMMs come last in the proposal's sequence. The novelty should not be claimed for the protected set: buildmer's include= and lme4's isSingular documentation ('keep it maximal ... removing only terms required') already cover it. What is new is the outcome-free ladder, the plan contract and their validation.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Release 1: the ladder generator, per-rung identifiability, localised SR-P, SR-none and protected LRT(.2), the plan hash with preregistration text, and a plain log. Defer masking, hash chains and GLMM rules. Paper 1: Gaussian LMMs (H1, H2, H3, H5). GLMMs (H4, H9) in a follow-up.

missed_considerations: SR-P as specified tests rank deficiency over all covariance blocks, so a protected slope at zero makes it strip non-zero nuisance slopes. In v2 this happened in 40-45% of data sets, costing up to 2.6 power points. The test has to be localised to unprotected terms (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lmecheck/76ff8921-f521-5c13-b469-59b514d4e510/scratchpad/r2/B-verify/scripts/v2_srp_global_vs_local.R).

In v2, localised SR-P, protected LRT(.2) and protected AIC behaved the same (differences of at most .005). The protected set does the work, and the choice of default rule among protected rules is a judgement call.

A singular fit is not a fitting failure (lme4 documentation). Stepping down a fixed ladder because of a zero-variance direction removes other, non-zero terms. Dropping exactly the zero directions, or keeping them, is the principled option; stepping down should be reserved for non-convergence.

The switching rule ('any cell > .06') needs multiplicity control and a relative reference. With 2,000 replicates and 50 cells, P(at least one exceedance) is .63 for a rule whose true rate is .05, and in v2 the ceiling itself reached .061.

The HPC budget omits Kenward-Roger (about 21 s per fit at n = 1,536) and parametric-bootstrap inference (about 95 CPU-hours per cell). See /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lmecheck/76ff8921-f521-5c13-b469-59b514d4e510/scratchpad/r2/B-verify/out/v3_cost_and_multiplicity.txt.

The protected rung behaves differently across engines. glmmTMB often has a non-positive-definite Hessian and NA standard errors at singular fits. In lme4 2.1-0, cs() with zero variances returns NA correlations with a warning.

Sim 1 is a single balanced, complete Latin-square design with Gaussian outcomes and +-0.5 coding. There is no evidence yet for unbalanced or missing data, or for the few-cluster education designs the user cares most about (H5).

The ladder depends on roles the user declares. Declaring every effect a nuisance yields an aggressive ladder, so the plan should record the role declarations and the report should flag an empty protected set.
The power comparisons are not size-adjusted. Report size-adjusted power, or report power next to the realised Type I error.
The claim that no published simulation evaluates a singular-triggered rule conflicts with the report's own extraction of Oberpriller et al. (2022).

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q1
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning:
The core strategy follows from the evidence: an engine-agnostic contract, a suite-owned IR and objective, a bring-your-own-estimates path, a statsmodels adapter for fits users already have, and no hard dependency on pymer4, juliacall or gpboost. I reproduced that evidence independently. My own implementation of the objective (marginal form for LMMs, b-scale form for Laplace and AGQ) matches A's to within 4.4e-11 on all 52 lme4 and glmmTMB estimate sets. Fresh fits of glmm 0.8.0 and mixedlm 1.3.0, using my own adapters, reach the best objective on 27 of 27 models (largest gaps 5.5e-9 and 5.9e-11). A search from 200 random starts confirms that this best value is the global optimum on all five small designs tested. statsmodels rejects weights with a ValueError.

Four parts need changing.
(i) The statsmodels evidence is overstated. With use_sparse=True, the crossed variance-component fits take 2.7 to 2.8 s for 2,400 rows and 23.6 s for 12,000 rows, against 0.11 to 0.86 s for lme4 in the same container. That is about 25x slower, not 130 to 313x. MixedLM can simulate, through get_distribution().rvs. A Gaussian offset can be absorbed into y. Stopping short of the optimum depends on the optimiser: Nelder-Mead reached the optimum on 3 of the 4 boundary designs, no setting did on the J <= q design, and lbfgs reported converged=True at gaps of 0.06 to 0.22.
(ii) Scope for one maintainer. Version 1 would ship three adapters, a Laplace and AGQ evaluator and weekly CI against two single-maintainer upstreams. The proposal stages GLMMs last.
(iii) The rpy2 CI bridge reintroduces the rpy2-to-R-version coupling the report itself documents, and adds nothing over Rscript-generated JSON fixtures.
(iv) The objective-match gate as specified would stop Stream A on valid lme4 1.1-35.1 Laplace fits (see Q1.contract).
recommendation_verdicts.change:
Version 1 covers Gaussian LMMs only, with three parts:
- A sparse ML and REML evaluator with weights and offsets.
- A statsmodels adapter that uses use_sparse=True for variance-component layouts, handles a Gaussian offset as y minus offset and records the optimiser used.
- The bring-your-own JSON protocol.

Ship at most one experimental Rust adapter in version 1, chosen by a pre-declared rule: fewest contract fields the suite must reconstruct, no Python-API break in the last 3 releases, then label fidelity and wheel coverage. The evidence is mixed.
- glmm keeps factor labels, follows lme4's rule for dropping aliased columns and is 8 to 14x faster than lme4. But it exposes no Z and no objective callable, ships fewer wheels and is LGPL.
- mixedlm exposes X, Z, theta and an objective callable, ships more wheels and is MIT. But it loses factor labels (f.1) and drops a different aliased column from lme4.

Add the Laplace and AGQ evaluator and the GLMM adapters at the GLMM stage. Replace the rpy2 CI bridge with Rscript-to-JSON fixtures. Consider an optional Rscript-subprocess adapter that fits through the suite's own R package, for Python users who have R.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q1.later
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning:
The promotion criteria are explicit and pre-declared, and the churn evidence supports them. mixedlm 1.3.0 changed its default optimiser and its GLMM estimation. It also fixed correctness bugs: nested fits had omitted parent factors, GLMM log-likelihoods lacked constants, and NLopt stopped up to 0.1 deviance units short. glmm releases roughly weekly. A small verification optimiser is feasible: Nelder-Mead followed by L-BFGS-B on the profiled objective found the global optimum from 200 of 200 random starts on every small design.

Weak points:
- Rejecting MixedModels.jl partly because it has no denominator df is inconsistent: statsmodels also has none, and the suite can compute Satterthwaite df from its own evaluator.
- glmm's breaking removals in 0.7.0 and 0.8.0 were almost all in the Rust crate API. The 0.8.0 changelog says 'The Python and R fits keep their fields and shapes', so the churn risk for a Python adapter is lower than stated.
- There is no fallback if no engine ever gains a second maintainer.
- Recomputing GLMM SEs needs the Laplace Hessian, and lme4 2.1-0 changed GLMM SEs (the stale-factor fix).
recommendation_verdicts.change: Keep the promotion criteria. Add a fallback: if no engine qualifies, the bring-your-own path and the R route remain the supported GLMM path in Python. Measure the 12-month stability criterion on the Python API and on conformance results, not on the Rust crate. Drop 'no denominator df' as a reason against MixedModels.jl. Schedule GLMM vcov recomputation for the GLMM stage, and regenerate the SE tiers with lme4 2.1-0 or later. Treat fastglmm on CRAN as a plausible trigger: glmm's CI notes that a vendored CRAN tarball is checked by hand with --as-cran.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q1.contract
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning:
The required fields are well motivated, and I confirmed the discrepancies behind them:
- A row-major reading of glmm's 3x3 varcorr shifts the REML criterion by +2.316 units and still yields a positive-definite matrix, so only an objective check catches it.
- glmmTMB's Gaussian weights equal replicating rows (sigma 0.8496 both ways), and current source still multiplies the log-likelihood by the weights.
- gpboost's default likelihood is off by 0.08 to 0.69 units.
- SE conventions differ by 2.4% for an LMM and by up to 2.2% for GLMMs.
- glmm postvar and statsmodels random_effects_cov equal the exact beta-fixed conditional variance to within 1e-14.

The gate itself is too brittle. Applied to A's own benchmark, the rule max(1e-6*|dev|, 1e-6) flags lme4 1.1-35.1's Laplace fits as contract_mismatch, through both R and rpy2: cbpp at 5.6e-4 against a tolerance of 1.8e-4, and binxd at 1.6e-3 against 1.4e-3. The R reference engine would therefore stop Stream A. lme4's own deviance function reproduces its reported value, which fits the stale-factor Laplace fixed in lme4 2.1-0. A missing reported objective has no defined outcome: glmmTMB on crossed_ML and jq_REML, and statsmodels' Bayesian fits. A confidence of 'high' is not warranted.
recommendation_verdicts.change:
- Set tolerances per criterion and engine version from the registry. Keep max(1e-6*|dev|, 1e-6) for LMMs. For Laplace and AGQ use something like max(1e-5*|dev|, 1e-2), plus registered offsets such as the missing AGQ constants and the stale-factor Laplace in lme4 before 2.1-0.
- Add the statuses objective_unavailable and objective_offset_registered in place of a hard stop. Stop only above the semantic-error scale: the smallest semantic error observed was 0.08 units.
- Let the adapter map weight semantics. glmmTMB's dispformula offset(-log w) reproduces lme4's precision weights exactly in 1.1.8; from 1.1.9 the Gaussian dispersion is on the SD scale, so the offset becomes -0.5*log w.
- Label the two conditional variances separately: the PEV that includes beta uncertainty differs from the beta-fixed variance by up to 24% on sleepstudy, not 1.7%.
- Lower confidence to medium until the HPC conformance runs.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q1.tiers
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning:
Assigning tiers per engine, version range and output class from a conformance corpus, objective first, fits the proposal's parity principle and my reproduction. The current table has inconsistencies:
- lme4 1.1-35 GLMM fits are in the tolerance tier on the common objective but fail the contract's objective-match rule.
- The statsmodels boundary tier depends on the optimiser (default against Nelder-Mead).
- statsmodels is 'unavailable for offsets' only for GLMMs.
- glmmTMB weights are called a different model, although a dispformula mapping reproduces lme4.
- The gpboost ranges disagree within the report (0.13 to 0.67 in one place, 0.08 to 0.6 in another; I measured 0.08 to 0.69).
- Every assignment rests on one replicate and on Ubuntu's lme4 1.1-35.1 and glmmTMB 1.1.8. Both are superseded in ways that change GLMM objectives and SEs (lme4 2.1-0) and the Gaussian dispersion scale (glmmTMB 1.1.9).
recommendation_verdicts.change: Add optimiser settings and the adapter mapping to the tier keys. Resolve the conflict between the objective-match rule and the tier rule. Mark every current assignment provisional, and regenerate the table on ARC from current CRAN and PyPI versions, with replicates, before it ships or is published.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q1.validation-paper
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning:
This matches the maintainer's yes to HPC validation and a paper. Objective-first conformance with Monte Carlo SEs is sound, and my 200-start search shows the best-known optimum can be certified cheaply for small q.

Missing points:
(a) Prior art. glmm already validates against a 947-cell grid, objective first against the best of several oracles, with a registry of explained divergences. The paper's contribution must therefore be the diagnostic contract and the design audits, with conformance as supporting evidence.
(b) Fixture licensing. sleepstudy, Penicillin, Pastes and cbpp come from lme4 (GPL >= 2) and Owls from glmmTMB, while the repository is MIT.
(c) 'Revisit if: never' should become a corpus versioned with the registry.
(d) The failure-rate estimand needs a pre-specified definition of the optimum: the best across engines plus a multi-start search for small q.
recommendation_verdicts.change:

- Version the corpus together with the registry.
- Cite glmm's validation grid as related work, and consider sharing fixtures.
- Preregister how the optimum is certified, the tolerances and a 'near threshold' status.

glmmTMB can reproduce lme4's precision weights through dispformula offset(-log w). From version 1.1.9 the Gaussian dispersion is on the SD scale, so the offset becomes -0.5*log w; the registry should record that dependence.

The reference evaluator must be sparse to reach the HPC sizes (A's prototype is dense, n x q). Scope: the proposal stages GLMMs last, but version 1 as recommended includes Laplace and AGQ and two experimental adapters. With BYO available, ship at most one experimental adapter in version 1.

My attempt to build lme4 2.1-0 from the CRAN GitHub mirror into a private library was denied by the permission classifier, so this is left for the local session.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q2 (version 1 model scope)
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The core decision fits the proposal's sequencing and per-output parity rule, and it is realistic for one maintainer: Stream A for Gaussian LMMs only, engine-free Stream B audits for every outcome type. Four supporting points are weaker than stated. (1) Usage. The cited reviews count LMM or multilevel papers but, as C read their abstracts, do not compare Gaussian with non-Gaussian outcomes. Agent B's extraction of the Meteyard & Davies abstract shows only n = 163 and n = 400. Only Bono et al. gives family shares, and none of these papers could be checked here. (2) C's warning-rate contrast is confounded with information. I reproduced C's 30 replicates exactly and extended them to 100. lmer gave 14%, Bernoulli glmer 59% and glmmTMB Bernoulli 67%. lmer with residual SD π/√3 (the logistic latent SD) and the same random-effect SDs gave 52% (Wilson 42–62%). Bernoulli with doubled random-effect SDs fell to 31%. So singular-fit triage is core v1.0 work for Gaussian models, and adding Bernoulli glmer triage in R costs less than C implies. (3) Exact parity of the separation LP is not automatic. In a degenerate example, three HiGHS settings returned three different optimal vertices, and the optimal face contained zero for two coefficients. A solver's vertex is therefore not a canonical output. (4) The LP relates y to X, so it is T2 and must be deferred in outcome-blind mode.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Keep Stream A v1.0 Gaussian-only, with these changes. (a) Limit v1.0 adapters to lme4 objects (lmerMod, lmerModLmerTest, afex) and statsmodels MixedLM. Move glmmTMB gaussian to v1.1 alongside the glmmTMB GLMM adapter. (b) Define the separation output as a verdict plus per-coefficient minimum and maximum over the optimal face, with tolerances in the registry, and require scipy >= 1.9. (c) Write down a decision rule. If the maintainer's own accuracy data need it before v1.1, add R-only Bernoulli and binomial glmer reporting and triage, delegate residual checks to DHARMa in Suggests, and return not_available in Python. (d) Release Stream B to CRAN and PyPI as 0.x rather than GitHub only. (e) Soften the 'Gaussian LMMs dominate' wording until the review tables are read.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q2 (roadmap after v1.0)
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The order is sound (binomial and Poisson first, then other families, then structured covariance, each promoted only after HPC validation), but several supporting claims fail. (1) 'Everything after v1.1 is R-only' ignores documented Python engines. glmm 0.8.0 estimates NB theta in GLMMs and fits Gamma GLMMs. mixedlm 1.3.0 fits compound-symmetry and AR(1) random-effect covariances, the same structures C plans for R in v1.3. gpboost 1.8.0 (Apache-2.0, one C++ core on both CRAN and PyPI) fits beta, beta-binomial, NB1 and NB2, zero-inflated and hurdle likelihoods with crossed random effects, though its random slopes are independent. C's own matrix notes gpboost's beta support. (2) The NEWS proxy is refuted. Only 9 of performance's 33 'binomial/Poisson/GLMM' hits mention a mixed model or glmmTMB; 24 are plain-GLM entries. LMM-related wording (the lme4 pattern plus generic 'mixed model') gives 20. (3) The CPU-hour figures assume 200 bootstrap refits per replicate. Without refits, C's own column gives 1.4–12 CPU-h per grid, so compute is not the constraint; maintainer time is. Over 100 datasets the median glmer Bernoulli fit took 1.94 s, 11 times lmer. (4) The warning rates depend on the generating parameters and come from old engine versions.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Relabel v1.2 (NB2, Gamma, beta, zero-inflated and hurdle) and v1.3 (cs, ar1) as 'R first; Python only through an engine promoted under key A's rule', with glmm, mixedlm and gpboost as named candidates. Drop the NEWS-count evidence. Present CPU-h as an upper-bound scenario next to the no-refit cost, and gate releases on maintainer time. Change 'never' for Bayesian fits to 'not planned for 1.x'. Correct two version facts: lme4's ar1 arrived in 2.0-1 itself, and glmmTMB's ordinal family arrived in 1.1.15.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q5 (report architecture and formats)
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The main architecture follows the proposal: canonical JSON, a self-contained HTML report with no scripts and a print stylesheet, an engine-free .qmd export rendered by the user's own Quarto, and Quarto only in Suggests. I confirmed its supporting facts from primary sources: Quarto's bundled pandoc and Typst versions at five tags, pdf-standard and the veraPDF installer in 1.9, Typst 0.14 tagging PDFs by default, the KOMA tagging caveat, pandoc's docx alt text (1.17) and SVG fix (3.1.10), quarto R package 1.5.1 NEWS, CRAN policy revision 6985, the PyPI quarto-cli sdist that downloads binaries at build time, and the OSF schema fields. Five errors need fixing. (1) Quarto ignored fig-alt in docx until 1.11 (#5514). Typst also failed on images that had alt text and pixel sizes until 1.11 (#14947). A 1.9 floor therefore gives Word figures without the intended alt text, and 1.11.9 is only five days old. (2) Chromium's source shows tagged Save-as-PDF output disabled by default in 85 and 86 and always on from 87, not 85. (3) ACRO blocks .svg for custom outputs and plots, so SVG files in the export would fail automated output checking in a trusted research environment. (4) 'Exactly what Stream B produces' overstates: inference criteria, exclusions and missing-data rules are user declarations. (5) plotly 7.1.0 embeds plotly.js by default; the CDN load came from C's include_plotlyjs='cdn'. The data-embedding finding itself is correct.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Require Quarto >= 1.11 for docx and Typst exports, and below that warn and fall back to HTML. Ship PNG copies of the aggregated figures in the export for TRE output checking. Say the package 'should not' depend on quarto-cli (it also pulls jupyter and nbclient), rather than 'cannot'. Correct the Chrome version to 87 and the plotly CDN statement. Describe the preregistration block as Stream B outputs plus required user declarations.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q5 (privacy defaults for participant-level and children's data)
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: Several parts are well supported: shareable mode as the default, k counted on persons, no extremes, and an explicit internal mode. C's leakage results reproduce exactly. My attack without oracle knowledge, on a PNG with ordinary ticks, found the true five most extreme residuals within 0.04–0.13 units. ACRO's defaults are confirmed. The ONS, DfE, SDC Handbook, ICO and GDPR statements could not be checked here. The rule set has four gaps. (1) Quantile bands leak extremes when a bin holds about k subjects. With n = 10, the 5% quantile lies between the two smallest values (median 0.19 SD from the minimum) and the 10% quantile is 90% of the way from x(1) to x(2), which amounts to showing the minimum that the same rules forbid. (2) Rounding margins to base 5 while leaving the other cells exact lets an attacker narrow a lone suppressed cell to ±2. ACRO's own round mitigation rounds every cell and then recomputes margins. (3) q5_plot_types prints exact outlier counts ('3 residuals beyond 4 SD'), which conflicts with the '<10' rule. (4) Comparing audits on the raw and analysis samples, as the proposal requires, creates a differencing risk. The dominance rule applied to row shares is C's own inference.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Add a quantile rule: show quantile p only if n·min(p, 1−p) >= k subjects. 10/90% bands then need at least 100 subjects per bin and 5/95% bands at least 200; otherwise show the median and IQR or suppress. Use secondary suppression or round every cell, not margins only. Apply '<k' to every count, including outlier counts and raw-versus-analysis differences. Cite the UK GDPR and DPA 2018 (as amended) and the ICO guidance alongside the EU recitals. Keep the DPO and data-provider check and the HPC disclosure-attack tests.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q5 (plot types and rendering)
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The leakage results justify static aggregated figures. Drawing them as inline SVG from the shared view model avoids optional plotting dependencies and allows title and desc elements. Byte identity across languages, however, holds only when the aggregates are bit-identical. Quantiles, envelopes and sums computed separately in R and Python can differ in the last ulp and flip printf rounding, and simulation envelopes use different RNG streams. Hash tests therefore work only on shared-draw fixtures, which matches the proposal's own approach to simulation parity. A hand-built SVG layer (ticks, labels and legends without font metrics) is a real build cost for one maintainer.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Test figure parity by comparing parsed coordinates within a tolerance, with a near-threshold status, and keep hash tests for shared fixtures. Limit the SVG grammar to a few fixed layouts (band, bar, matrix) with an explicit effort budget. Apply the quantile rule from the privacy item. Verify Kleiber & Zeileis before citing them for rootograms.

recommendation_verdicts.question: Q5 (accessibility)
recommendation_verdicts.reasoning: The WCAG criterion texts, the 1.1.1 data-chart example and the contrast ratios against white are all confirmed from W3C source and by recomputation. Three gaps remain. (1) SC 1.4.11 requires 3:1 against adjacent colours, and the five essential colours reach only 1.12–1.69 against each other. The Understanding document relieves this when the values are also presented in a conforming way, which the mandatory data tables do. (2) Quarto's bundled axe-core 4.10.3 scans only documents that Quarto renders, so CI must run axe-core itself on the package's HTML. veraPDF also needs Java (8, 11, 17 or 21). (3) WCAG 2.2 was republished with errata on 12 December 2024. The UK monitoring claim could not be verified here.
recommendation_verdicts.change: Separate adjacent coloured areas with white gaps or outlines of at least 3:1 and use direct labels. Keep the data table mandatory for every figure. In CI, run axe-core from npm in a headless browser, plus an HTML validator. Cite the 12 December 2024 republication of WCAG 2.2. Keep screen-reader testing for the local session.
